ಕಲ್ಯಾಣದ ಚಾಲುಕ್ಯರು ಮತ್ತು ಅವರ ಕಾಲದ ಸಾಹಿತ್ಯ ವರ್ಣಿಸುವುದು
kn.hook: ಎಲ್ಲೋರಾದ ಕೈಲಾಸ ದೇವಾಲಯವನ್ನು ಒಂದೇ ಬಂಡೆಯಿಂದ ಮೇಲಿನಿಂದ ಕೆಳಕ್ಕೆ ಕೆತ್ತಲಾಗಿದೆ. ಯಾವ ಕರ್ನಾಟಕದ ರಾಜವಂಶ ಅದನ್ನು ನಿರ್ಮಿಸಿತು?
kn.example: ಅರಬ್ ಪ್ರವಾಸಿ ಸುಲೈಮಾನ್ ರಾಷ್ಟ್ರಕೂಟ ದೊರೆಯನ್ನು ಜಗತ್ತಿನ ನಾಲ್ಕು ಮಹಾ ರಾಜರಲ್ಲಿ ಒಬ್ಬ ಎಂದು ವರ್ಣಿಸಿದ.
kn.activity: ಕನ್ನಡ ಸಾಹಿತ್ಯ ಕಾಲರೇಖೆ: ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಕವಿರಾಜಮಾರ್ಗ, ಪಂಪ, ರನ್ನ, ವಚನಗಳನ್ನು ಕಾಲರೇಖೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಇಡುತ್ತಾರೆ.
kn.homework: ಕವಿರಾಜಮಾರ್ಗ ಕನ್ನಡಕ್ಕೆ ಏಕೆ ಮುಖ್ಯ ಬರೆ.

chapters.title: The Cholas and the Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra

topics.title: The Cholas and the Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra
topics.summary: Rajaraja I built the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur; his son Rajendra I sent a navy to Southeast Asia.
notes: Rajaraja I built the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur; his son Rajendra I sent a navy to Southeast Asia.
Chola villages had assemblies (sabhas); the Uttaramerur inscriptions describe elections by the kudavolai (pot-ticket) system.
The Hoysalas ruled from Dwarasamudra (Halebidu); Vishnuvardhana was a great king who followed Ramanujacharya's teaching.
Hoysala temples at Belur (Chennakeshava), Halebidu (Hoysaleshwara) and Somanathapura are star-shaped with fine soapstone carvings.
outcomes: Describe the Chola empire, its navy and local self-government
Describe the Hoysalas and their temple architecture

lesson.hook: A thousand years ago, Chola villages elected their committees by drawing names from a pot. What does that remind you of?
lesson.example: The Chennakeshava temple at Belur took about 103 years to complete, and its bracket figures (madanikas) are famous.
lesson.activity: Village election role play: children elect a committee by the kudavolai system and compare it with a secret ballot today.

questions.a: Electing village committee members by drawing palm-leaf tickets from a pot.
Belur Chennakeshava, Halebidu Hoysaleshwara or Somanathapura (any two).

lesson.homework: Draw the star-shaped plan of a Hoysala temple and label its parts.

kn.title: ಚೋಳರು ಮತ್ತು ದ್ವಾರಸಮುದ್ರದ ಹೊಯ್ಸಳರು
notes: ಒಂದನೇ ರಾಜರಾಜ ತಂಜಾವೂರಿನ ಬೃಹದೀಶ್ವರ ದೇವಾಲಯ ಕಟ್ಟಿಸಿದ; ಅವನ ಮಗ ಒಂದನೇ ರಾಜೇಂದ್ರ ಆಗ್ನೇಯ ಏಷ್ಯಾಕ್ಕೆ ನೌಕಾಪಡೆ ಕಳುಹಿಸಿದ.
ಚೋಳರ ಹಳ್ಳಿಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಸಭೆಗಳಿದ್ದವು; ಉತ್ತರಮೇರೂರು ಶಾಸನಗಳು ಕುಡವೋಲೈ (ಮಡಕೆ-ಚೀಟಿ) ಪದ್ಧತಿಯ ಚುನಾವಣೆ ವರ್ಣಿಸುತ್ತವೆ.
ಹೊಯ್ಸಳರು ದ್ವಾರಸಮುದ್ರದಿಂದ (ಹಳೇಬೀಡು) ಆಳಿದರು; ರಾಮಾನುಜಾಚಾರ್ಯರ ಬೋಧನೆ ಅನುಸರಿಸಿದ ವಿಷ್ಣುವರ್ಧನ ಶ್ರೇಷ್ಠ ದೊರೆ.
ಬೇಲೂರು (ಚೆನ್ನಕೇಶವ), ಹಳೇಬೀಡು (ಹೊಯ್ಸಳೇಶ್ವರ), ಸೋಮನಾಥಪುರದ ಹೊಯ್ಸಳ ದೇವಾಲಯಗಳು ನಕ್ಷತ್ರಾಕಾರ, ಸೂಕ್ಷ್ಮ ಬಳಪದ ಕಲ್ಲಿನ ಕೆತ್ತನೆ.
outcomes: ಚೋಳ ಸಾಮ್ರಾಜ್ಯ, ಅದರ ನೌಕಾಪಡೆ ಮತ್ತು ಸ್ಥಳೀಯ ಸ್ವಯಂ ಆಡಳಿತ ವರ್ಣಿಸುವುದು
ಹೊಯ್ಸಳರು ಮತ್ತು ಅವರ ದೇವಾಲಯ ವಾಸ್ತುಶಿಲ್ಪ ವರ್ಣಿಸುವುದು
kn.hook: ಸಾವಿರ ವರ್ಷ ಹಿಂದೆ ಚೋಳರ ಹಳ್ಳಿಗಳು ಮಡಕೆಯಿಂದ ಹೆಸರು ತೆಗೆದು ತಮ್ಮ ಸಮಿತಿ ಆರಿಸುತ್ತಿದ್ದವು. ಅದು ನಿನಗೆ ಏನನ್ನು ನೆನಪಿಸುತ್ತದೆ?
kn.example: ಬೇಲೂರಿನ ಚೆನ್ನಕೇಶವ ದೇವಾಲಯ ಪೂರ್ಣಗೊಳ್ಳಲು ಸುಮಾರು 103 ವರ್ಷ ಬೇಕಾಯಿತು, ಅದರ ಮದನಿಕೆಗಳು ಪ್ರಸಿದ್ಧ.
kn.activity: ಹಳ್ಳಿ ಚುನಾವಣೆ ಅಭಿನಯ: ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಕುಡವೋಲೈ ಪದ್ಧತಿಯಿಂದ ಸಮಿತಿ ಆರಿಸಿ ಇಂದಿನ ಗುಪ್ತ ಮತದಾನದೊಂದಿಗೆ ಹೋಲಿಸುತ್ತಾರೆ.

questions.a: ಮಡಕೆಯಿಂದ ತಾಳೆಗರಿ ಚೀಟಿ ತೆಗೆದು ಹಳ್ಳಿ ಸಮಿತಿ ಸದಸ್ಯರನ್ನು ಆರಿಸುವುದು.
ಬೇಲೂರು ಚೆನ್ನಕೇಶವ, ಹಳೇಬೀಡು ಹೊಯ್ಸಳೇಶ್ವರ ಅಥವಾ ಸೋಮನಾಥಪುರ (ಯಾವುದಾದರೂ ಎರಡು).

kn.homework: ಹೊಯ್ಸಳ ದೇವಾಲಯದ ನಕ್ಷತ್ರಾಕಾರದ ನಕ್ಷೆ ಬಿಡಿಸಿ ಭಾಗಗಳನ್ನು ಹೆಸರಿಸು.

topics.title: Democracy
topics.summary: Democracy means rule by the people; it may be direct (people decide themselves) or indirect/representative (people elect representatives).
notes: Democracy means rule by the people; it may be direct (people decide themselves) or indirect/representative (people elect representatives).
Features: free and fair elections, universal adult franchise, rule of law, rights and freedoms, an independent judiciary and a free press.
Merits: equality, protection of rights, peaceful change of government and people's participation.
Success needs literacy, awareness, tolerance, honest leaders and active citizens; threats include poverty, corruption and communalism.
outcomes: Explain the meaning, types and features of democracy
Discuss the merits of democracy and the conditions for its success

lesson.hook: Why do citizens of a democracy sometimes argue loudly with their government — and why is that a good sign?
lesson.example: Switzerland still uses direct democracy in some cantons, where citizens vote directly on laws in open-air assemblies.
lesson.activity: Class parliament: children debate a school rule, with a ruling side and an opposition, and then vote.

questions.a: People elect representatives who govern on their behalf.
Free elections, rule of law, rights, independent judiciary, free press (any two).

questions.q: Give one condition for the success of democracy.
questions.a: Literacy, awareness, tolerance, honest leadership (any one).

lesson.homework: Write how a free press helps democracy.

kn.title: ಪ್ರಜಾಪ್ರಭುತ್ವ
notes: ಪ್ರಜಾಪ್ರಭುತ್ವ ಎಂದರೆ ಜನರ ಆಳ್ವಿಕೆ; ನೇರ (ಜನರೇ ನಿರ್ಧರಿಸುತ್ತಾರೆ) ಅಥವಾ ಪರೋಕ್ಷ/ಪ್ರಾತಿನಿಧಿಕ (ಜನ ಪ್ರತಿನಿಧಿ ಆರಿಸುತ್ತಾರೆ).
ಲಕ್ಷಣಗಳು: ಮುಕ್ತ-ನ್ಯಾಯಸಮ್ಮತ ಚುನಾವಣೆ, ಸಾರ್ವತ್ರಿಕ ವಯಸ್ಕ ಮತದಾನ, ಕಾನೂನಿನ ಆಳ್ವಿಕೆ, ಹಕ್ಕು-ಸ್ವಾತಂತ್ರ್ಯ, ಸ್ವತಂತ್ರ ನ್ಯಾಯಾಂಗ, ಮುಕ್ತ ಪತ್ರಿಕೋದ್ಯಮ.
ಅನುಕೂಲ: ಸಮಾನತೆ, ಹಕ್ಕುಗಳ ರಕ್ಷಣೆ, ಸರ್ಕಾರದ ಶಾಂತಿಯುತ ಬದಲಾವಣೆ, ಜನರ ಭಾಗವಹಿಸುವಿಕೆ.
ಯಶಸ್ಸಿಗೆ ಸಾಕ್ಷರತೆ, ಜಾಗೃತಿ, ಸಹಿಷ್ಣುತೆ, ಪ್ರಾಮಾಣಿಕ ನಾಯಕರು, ಸಕ್ರಿಯ ಪೌರರು ಬೇಕು; ಬಡತನ, ಭ್ರಷ್ಟಾಚಾರ, ಕೋಮುವಾದ ಅಪಾಯಗಳು.
outcomes: ಪ್ರಜಾಪ್ರಭುತ್ವದ ಅರ್ಥ, ಪ್ರಕಾರ, ಲಕ್ಷಣ ವಿವರಿಸುವುದು
ಪ್ರಜಾಪ್ರಭುತ್ವದ ಅನುಕೂಲ ಮತ್ತು ಯಶಸ್ಸಿನ ಷರತ್ತು ಚರ್ಚಿಸುವುದು
kn.hook: ಪ್ರಜಾಪ್ರಭುತ್ವದ ಪೌರರು ಕೆಲವೊಮ್ಮೆ ಸರ್ಕಾರದೊಂದಿಗೆ ಜೋರಾಗಿ ವಾದಿಸುತ್ತಾರೆ — ಅದು ಏಕೆ ಒಳ್ಳೆಯ ಸಂಕೇತ?
kn.example: ಸ್ವಿಟ್ಜರ್ಲೆಂಡಿನ ಕೆಲವು ಪ್ರಾಂತ್ಯಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಪೌರರು ಬಯಲು ಸಭೆಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಕಾನೂನುಗಳಿಗೆ ನೇರವಾಗಿ ಮತ ಹಾಕುವ ನೇರ ಪ್ರಜಾಪ್ರಭುತ್ವ ಇನ್ನೂ ಇದೆ.
kn.activity: ತರಗತಿ ಸಂಸತ್ತು: ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಆಡಳಿತ ಮತ್ತು ವಿರೋಧ ಪಕ್ಷವಾಗಿ ಶಾಲಾ ನಿಯಮ ಚರ್ಚಿಸಿ ಮತ ಹಾಕುತ್ತಾರೆ.

questions.a: ಜನ ತಮ್ಮ ಪರವಾಗಿ ಆಳುವ ಪ್ರತಿನಿಧಿಗಳನ್ನು ಆರಿಸುತ್ತಾರೆ.
ಮುಕ್ತ ಚುನಾವಣೆ, ಕಾನೂನಿನ ಆಳ್ವಿಕೆ, ಹಕ್ಕು, ಸ್ವತಂತ್ರ ನ್ಯಾಯಾಂಗ, ಮುಕ್ತ ಪತ್ರಿಕೋದ್ಯಮ (ಯಾವುದಾದರೂ ಎರಡು).

kn.homework: ಮುಕ್ತ ಪತ್ರಿಕೋದ್ಯಮ ಪ್ರಜಾಪ್ರಭುತ್ವಕ್ಕೆ ಹೇಗೆ ನೆರವಾಗುತ್ತದೆ ಬರೆ.

topics.title: Local Self-Government
topics.summary: The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992) gave constitutional status to rural and urban local bodies.
notes: The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992) gave constitutional status to rural and urban local bodies.
Karnataka's three-tier Panchayat Raj (Karnataka Panchayat Raj Act, 1993): Gram Panchayat (village), Taluk Panchayat and Zilla Panchayat (district).
Urban bodies: Municipal Corporations (big cities like Bengaluru), City and Town Municipal Councils and Town Panchayats.
The Gram Sabha of all village voters reviews plans and chooses beneficiaries; Karnataka reserves 50% of seats in local bodies for women.
outcomes: Describe the three-tier Panchayat Raj system and urban local bodies
Explain the role of the Gram Sabha and reservation for women

lesson.hook: Who decides where the new borewell or streetlight in your village goes? Not Delhi or Bengaluru — someone much closer!
lesson.example: Local bodies look after drinking water, street lights, drains, village roads and birth and death registration.
lesson.activity: Gram Sabha role play: children hold a mock Gram Sabha to decide how to spend a small village budget.

questions.q: Name the three tiers of Panchayat Raj.
questions.a: Gram Panchayat, Taluk Panchayat and Zilla Panchayat.
The meeting of all voters of a village.

questions.q: What share of local-body seats is reserved for women in Karnataka?

lesson.homework: Find out the name of your Gram Panchayat or ward member and one work they have done.

kn.title: ಸ್ಥಳೀಯ ಸ್ವಯಂ ಸರ್ಕಾರ
notes: 73 ಮತ್ತು 74ನೇ ಸಂವಿಧಾನ ತಿದ್ದುಪಡಿ (1992) ಗ್ರಾಮೀಣ ಮತ್ತು ನಗರ ಸ್ಥಳೀಯ ಸಂಸ್ಥೆಗಳಿಗೆ ಸಾಂವಿಧಾನಿಕ ಸ್ಥಾನ ಕೊಟ್ಟಿತು.
ಕರ್ನಾಟಕದ ಮೂರು ಹಂತದ ಪಂಚಾಯತ್ ರಾಜ್ (ಕರ್ನಾಟಕ ಪಂಚಾಯತ್ ರಾಜ್ ಕಾಯ್ದೆ, 1993): ಗ್ರಾಮ ಪಂಚಾಯಿತಿ, ತಾಲೂಕು ಪಂಚಾಯಿತಿ, ಜಿಲ್ಲಾ ಪಂಚಾಯಿತಿ.
ನಗರ ಸಂಸ್ಥೆಗಳು: ಮಹಾನಗರ ಪಾಲಿಕೆ (ಬೆಂಗಳೂರಿನಂತಹ ದೊಡ್ಡ ನಗರ), ನಗರಸಭೆ, ಪುರಸಭೆ, ಪಟ್ಟಣ ಪಂಚಾಯಿತಿ.
ಗ್ರಾಮದ ಎಲ್ಲ ಮತದಾರರ ಗ್ರಾಮಸಭೆ ಯೋಜನೆ ಪರಿಶೀಲಿಸಿ ಫಲಾನುಭವಿ ಆರಿಸುತ್ತದೆ; ಕರ್ನಾಟಕ ಸ್ಥಳೀಯ ಸಂಸ್ಥೆಗಳಲ್ಲಿ 50% ಸ್ಥಾನ ಮಹಿಳೆಯರಿಗೆ ಮೀಸಲಿಡುತ್ತದೆ.
outcomes: ಮೂರು ಹಂತದ ಪಂಚಾಯತ್ ರಾಜ್ ಮತ್ತು ನಗರ ಸ್ಥಳೀಯ ಸಂಸ್ಥೆಗಳನ್ನು ವರ್ಣಿಸುವುದು
ಗ್ರಾಮಸಭೆಯ ಪಾತ್ರ ಮತ್ತು ಮಹಿಳಾ ಮೀಸಲಾತಿ ವಿವರಿಸುವುದು
kn.hook: ನಿನ್ನ ಹಳ್ಳಿಯ ಹೊಸ ಕೊಳವೆಬಾವಿ ಅಥವಾ ಬೀದಿದೀಪ ಎಲ್ಲಿ ಬರಬೇಕೆಂದು ನಿರ್ಧರಿಸುವವರು ಯಾರು? ದೆಹಲಿ ಅಥವಾ ಬೆಂಗಳೂರಲ್ಲ — ಬಹಳ ಹತ್ತಿರದವರು!
kn.example: ಸ್ಥಳೀಯ ಸಂಸ್ಥೆಗಳು ಕುಡಿಯುವ ನೀರು, ಬೀದಿದೀಪ, ಚರಂಡಿ, ಹಳ್ಳಿ ರಸ್ತೆ, ಜನನ-ಮರಣ ನೋಂದಣಿ ನೋಡಿಕೊಳ್ಳುತ್ತವೆ.
kn.activity: ಗ್ರಾಮಸಭೆ ಅಭಿನಯ: ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಅಣಕು ಗ್ರಾಮಸಭೆ ನಡೆಸಿ ಹಳ್ಳಿಯ ಸಣ್ಣ ಬಜೆಟ್ ಹೇಗೆ ಖರ್ಚು ಮಾಡಬೇಕು ನಿರ್ಧರಿಸುತ್ತಾರೆ.

questions.a: ಗ್ರಾಮ ಪಂಚಾಯಿತಿ, ತಾಲೂಕು ಪಂಚಾಯಿತಿ, ಜಿಲ್ಲಾ ಪಂಚಾಯಿತಿ.

questions.q: ಕರ್ನಾಟಕದಲ್ಲಿ ಸ್ಥಳೀಯ ಸಂಸ್ಥೆಗಳ ಎಷ್ಟು ಸ್ಥಾನ ಮಹಿಳೆಯರಿಗೆ ಮೀಸಲು?

kn.homework: ನಿನ್ನ ಗ್ರಾಮ ಪಂಚಾಯಿತಿ ಅಥವಾ ವಾರ್ಡ್ ಸದಸ್ಯರ ಹೆಸರು ಮತ್ತು ಅವರು ಮಾಡಿದ ಒಂದು ಕೆಲಸ ತಿಳಿದುಕೋ.

topics.title: Sociology in Everyday Life
topics.summary: Sociology is the scientific study of society and social relationships; Auguste Comte is called its father.
notes: Sociology is the scientific study of society and social relationships; Auguste Comte is called its father.
Everyday life is shaped by social groups (family, friends, school), each with its own roles and expectations.
Norms are rules of behaviour (folkways and customs); values are ideas of what is good and important.
Understanding society helps us respect differences, solve social problems and live together peacefully.
outcomes: Explain how sociology helps us understand everyday life
Describe social groups, roles, norms and values

lesson.hook: Why do you behave differently at a wedding, in a classroom and on a cricket field? Sociology has the answer.
lesson.example: A girl can be a daughter at home, a student at school and a captain on the field — the same person with different roles.
lesson.activity: Role map: each child draws themselves in the middle and lists all the roles they play and the groups they belong to.

questions.q: Who is called the father of Sociology?

questions.a: Rules of behaviour accepted by a group or society.

questions.q: Give an example of a social group.
questions.a: Family, friends, school class, sports team (any one).

lesson.homework: Write three norms followed in your home and why they exist.

kn.title: ದೈನಂದಿನ ಜೀವನದಲ್ಲಿ ಸಮಾಜಶಾಸ್ತ್ರ
notes: ಸಮಾಜ ಮತ್ತು ಸಾಮಾಜಿಕ ಸಂಬಂಧಗಳ ವೈಜ್ಞಾನಿಕ ಅಧ್ಯಯನ ಸಮಾಜಶಾಸ್ತ್ರ; ಆಗಸ್ಟ್ ಕಾಮ್ಟ್ ಅದರ ಪಿತಾಮಹ.
ದೈನಂದಿನ ಜೀವನವನ್ನು ಸಾಮಾಜಿಕ ಗುಂಪುಗಳು (ಕುಟುಂಬ, ಸ್ನೇಹಿತರು, ಶಾಲೆ) ರೂಪಿಸುತ್ತವೆ, ಪ್ರತಿಯೊಂದಕ್ಕೂ ತನ್ನದೇ ಪಾತ್ರ ಮತ್ತು ನಿರೀಕ್ಷೆ.
ನಿಯಮಗಳು ವರ್ತನೆಯ ನಿಯಮ (ಜನಾಚಾರ, ಸಂಪ್ರದಾಯ); ಮೌಲ್ಯಗಳು ಒಳ್ಳೆಯದು-ಮುಖ್ಯವಾದುದರ ಬಗೆಗಿನ ವಿಚಾರ.
ಸಮಾಜ ಅರಿಯುವುದು ವ್ಯತ್ಯಾಸ ಗೌರವಿಸಲು, ಸಾಮಾಜಿಕ ಸಮಸ್ಯೆ ಬಗೆಹರಿಸಲು, ಶಾಂತಿಯಿಂದ ಒಟ್ಟಿಗೆ ಬದುಕಲು ನೆರವಾಗುತ್ತದೆ.
outcomes: ಸಮಾಜಶಾಸ್ತ್ರ ದೈನಂದಿನ ಜೀವನ ಅರಿಯಲು ಹೇಗೆ ನೆರವಾಗುತ್ತದೆ ವಿವರಿಸುವುದು
ಸಾಮಾಜಿಕ ಗುಂಪು, ಪಾತ್ರ, ನಿಯಮ, ಮೌಲ್ಯ ವರ್ಣಿಸುವುದು
kn.hook: ಮದುವೆಯಲ್ಲಿ, ತರಗತಿಯಲ್ಲಿ, ಕ್ರಿಕೆಟ್ ಮೈದಾನದಲ್ಲಿ ನೀನು ಬೇರೆ ಬೇರೆ ರೀತಿ ವರ್ತಿಸುವುದೇಕೆ? ಸಮಾಜಶಾಸ್ತ್ರದಲ್ಲಿ ಉತ್ತರವಿದೆ.
kn.example: ಒಬ್ಬ ಹುಡುಗಿ ಮನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಮಗಳು, ಶಾಲೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ವಿದ್ಯಾರ್ಥಿನಿ, ಮೈದಾನದಲ್ಲಿ ನಾಯಕಿ — ಒಂದೇ ವ್ಯಕ್ತಿ, ಬೇರೆ ಪಾತ್ರಗಳು.
kn.activity: ಪಾತ್ರ ನಕ್ಷೆ: ಪ್ರತಿ ಮಗು ತನ್ನನ್ನು ಮಧ್ಯದಲ್ಲಿ ಬಿಡಿಸಿ ತಾನು ನಿರ್ವಹಿಸುವ ಎಲ್ಲ ಪಾತ್ರ ಮತ್ತು ಸೇರಿದ ಗುಂಪುಗಳನ್ನು ಪಟ್ಟಿ ಮಾಡುತ್ತದೆ.

questions.a: ಗುಂಪು ಅಥವಾ ಸಮಾಜ ಒಪ್ಪಿದ ವರ್ತನೆಯ ನಿಯಮಗಳು.
ಕುಟುಂಬ, ಸ್ನೇಹಿತರು, ಶಾಲಾ ತರಗತಿ, ಕ್ರೀಡಾ ತಂಡ (ಯಾವುದಾದರೂ).

kn.homework: ನಿನ್ನ ಮನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಪಾಲಿಸುವ ಮೂರು ನಿಯಮ ಮತ್ತು ಅವು ಏಕಿವೆ ಬರೆ.

topics.title: Types of Society
topics.summary: Tribal society: small, close-knit communities living in forests or hills, with their own language, customs and dependence on nature (e.g. Soligas, Jenu Kurubas).
notes: Tribal society: small, close-knit communities living in forests or hills, with their own language, customs and dependence on nature (e.g. Soligas, Jenu Kurubas).
Rural society: villages where most people farm; strong family and neighbourhood ties, joint families and traditions.
Urban society: towns and cities with large populations, varied jobs, nuclear families, more services and faster change.
Education, transport, media and migration are bringing social change in all three.
outcomes: Describe tribal, rural and urban societies
Compare their features and explain social change

lesson.hook: A family in a Soliga forest hamlet, a farmer's family in a Mandya village and a family in a Bengaluru apartment — how are their lives different?
lesson.example: The Soligas of the Biligiri Rangana Hills collect honey and forest produce and have deep knowledge of the forest.
lesson.activity: Three-column chart: groups compare housing, occupations, family type and festivals in tribal, rural and urban societies.

questions.q: Name a tribal community of Karnataka.
questions.a: Soliga, Jenu Kuruba, Kadu Kuruba or Siddi (any one).

questions.q: What is the main occupation in rural society?
Give one feature of urban society.
questions.a: Large population, varied jobs, nuclear families, more services (any one).

lesson.homework: Interview someone who moved from a village to a town and write how their life changed.

kn.title: ಸಮಾಜದ ಪ್ರಕಾರಗಳು
notes: ಬುಡಕಟ್ಟು ಸಮಾಜ: ಕಾಡು-ಬೆಟ್ಟಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ವಾಸಿಸುವ, ತಮ್ಮದೇ ಭಾಷೆ, ಸಂಪ್ರದಾಯ, ನಿಸರ್ಗದ ಮೇಲೆ ಅವಲಂಬನೆಯಿರುವ ಸಣ್ಣ ಆಪ್ತ ಸಮುದಾಯಗಳು (ಉದಾ: ಸೋಲಿಗರು, ಜೇನುಕುರುಬರು).
ಗ್ರಾಮೀಣ ಸಮಾಜ: ಹೆಚ್ಚಿನವರು ಕೃಷಿ ಮಾಡುವ ಹಳ್ಳಿಗಳು; ಬಲವಾದ ಕುಟುಂಬ-ನೆರೆಹೊರೆ ಸಂಬಂಧ, ಅವಿಭಕ್ತ ಕುಟುಂಬ, ಸಂಪ್ರದಾಯ.
ನಗರ ಸಮಾಜ: ಹೆಚ್ಚು ಜನಸಂಖ್ಯೆ, ವಿವಿಧ ಉದ್ಯೋಗ, ವಿಭಕ್ತ ಕುಟುಂಬ, ಹೆಚ್ಚು ಸೇವೆ, ವೇಗದ ಬದಲಾವಣೆಯ ಪಟ್ಟಣ-ನಗರಗಳು.
ಶಿಕ್ಷಣ, ಸಾರಿಗೆ, ಮಾಧ್ಯಮ, ವಲಸೆ ಮೂರರಲ್ಲೂ ಸಾಮಾಜಿಕ ಬದಲಾವಣೆ ತರುತ್ತಿವೆ.
outcomes: ಬುಡಕಟ್ಟು, ಗ್ರಾಮೀಣ, ನಗರ ಸಮಾಜಗಳನ್ನು ವರ್ಣಿಸುವುದು
ಅವುಗಳ ಲಕ್ಷಣ ಹೋಲಿಸಿ ಸಾಮಾಜಿಕ ಬದಲಾವಣೆ ವಿವರಿಸುವುದು
kn.hook: ಸೋಲಿಗರ ಕಾಡಿನ ಹಾಡಿಯ ಕುಟುಂಬ, ಮಂಡ್ಯದ ಹಳ್ಳಿಯ ರೈತ ಕುಟುಂಬ, ಬೆಂಗಳೂರಿನ ಅಪಾರ್ಟ್‌ಮೆಂಟ್‌ನ ಕುಟುಂಬ — ಅವರ ಜೀವನ ಹೇಗೆ ಬೇರೆ?
kn.example: ಬಿಳಿಗಿರಿರಂಗನ ಬೆಟ್ಟದ ಸೋಲಿಗರು ಜೇನು ಮತ್ತು ಕಾಡಿನ ಉತ್ಪನ್ನ ಸಂಗ್ರಹಿಸುತ್ತಾರೆ, ಕಾಡಿನ ಬಗ್ಗೆ ಆಳವಾದ ಜ್ಞಾನ ಹೊಂದಿದ್ದಾರೆ.
kn.activity: ಮೂರು ಕಾಲಂ ಚಾರ್ಟ್: ಗುಂಪುಗಳು ಬುಡಕಟ್ಟು, ಗ್ರಾಮೀಣ, ನಗರ ಸಮಾಜಗಳ ವಸತಿ, ಉದ್ಯೋಗ, ಕುಟುಂಬ ಬಗೆ, ಹಬ್ಬ ಹೋಲಿಸುತ್ತವೆ.

questions.a: ಹೆಚ್ಚು ಜನಸಂಖ್ಯೆ, ವಿವಿಧ ಉದ್ಯೋಗ, ವಿಭಕ್ತ ಕುಟುಂಬ, ಹೆಚ್ಚು ಸೇವೆ (ಯಾವುದಾದರೂ).

kn.homework: ಹಳ್ಳಿಯಿಂದ ಪಟ್ಟಣಕ್ಕೆ ಬಂದ ಒಬ್ಬರನ್ನು ಸಂದರ್ಶಿಸಿ ಅವರ ಜೀವನ ಹೇಗೆ ಬದಲಾಯಿತು ಬರೆ.

topics.title: Hydrosphere
topics.summary: The hydrosphere includes oceans, seas, rivers, lakes, groundwater and ice; the Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean.
notes: The hydrosphere includes oceans, seas, rivers, lakes, groundwater and ice; the Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean.
The ocean floor has a continental shelf, continental slope, deep-sea plains, ridges and trenches (the Mariana Trench is the deepest).
Salinity is the amount of salt in sea water (average about 35 parts per thousand).
Ocean currents are large streams of moving water (warm and cold); tides are the regular rise and fall of the sea caused mainly by the Moon's pull.
outcomes: Describe the oceans and the relief of the ocean floor
Explain salinity, ocean currents and tides

lesson.hook: About 71% of the Earth's surface is water, yet we call our planet 'Earth'. What lies beneath the oceans?
lesson.example: Fishing is rich on continental shelves, which are shallow and receive plenty of sunlight for plankton to grow.
lesson.activity: Salt water test: children dissolve salt in water and float an egg to see how salinity changes buoyancy.

questions.a: Mainly the gravitational pull of the Moon (and the Sun).
The amount of salt in sea water.

lesson.homework: Draw a labelled diagram of the ocean floor.

kn.title: ಜಲಗೋಳ
notes: ಜಲಗೋಳದಲ್ಲಿ ಸಾಗರ, ಸಮುದ್ರ, ನದಿ, ಸರೋವರ, ಅಂತರ್ಜಲ, ಹಿಮ ಸೇರಿವೆ; ಪೆಸಿಫಿಕ್ ಅತಿ ದೊಡ್ಡ ಮತ್ತು ಆಳವಾದ ಸಾಗರ.
ಸಾಗರ ತಳದಲ್ಲಿ ಖಂಡಾವರಣ ಪ್ರದೇಶ, ಖಂಡಾವರಣ ಇಳಿಜಾರು, ಆಳ ಸಾಗರ ಬಯಲು, ಏಣು, ಕಂದಕಗಳಿವೆ (ಮರಿಯಾನಾ ಕಂದಕ ಅತಿ ಆಳ).
ಲವಣತೆ ಸಮುದ್ರದ ನೀರಿನಲ್ಲಿರುವ ಉಪ್ಪಿನ ಪ್ರಮಾಣ (ಸರಾಸರಿ ಸಾವಿರಕ್ಕೆ ಸುಮಾರು 35 ಭಾಗ).
ಸಾಗರ ಪ್ರವಾಹಗಳು ಚಲಿಸುವ ನೀರಿನ ದೊಡ್ಡ ಹರಿವು (ಬೆಚ್ಚನೆ ಮತ್ತು ತಣ್ಣನೆ); ಉಬ್ಬರವಿಳಿತ ಮುಖ್ಯವಾಗಿ ಚಂದ್ರನ ಸೆಳೆತದಿಂದ ಸಮುದ್ರದ ನಿಯಮಿತ ಏರಿಳಿತ.
outcomes: ಸಾಗರಗಳು ಮತ್ತು ಸಾಗರ ತಳದ ಭೂಸ್ವರೂಪ ವರ್ಣಿಸುವುದು
ಲವಣತೆ, ಸಾಗರ ಪ್ರವಾಹ, ಉಬ್ಬರವಿಳಿತ ವಿವರಿಸುವುದು
kn.hook: ಭೂಮಿಯ ಮೇಲ್ಮೈಯ ಸುಮಾರು 71% ನೀರು, ಆದರೂ ನಮ್ಮ ಗ್ರಹವನ್ನು 'ಭೂಮಿ' ಎನ್ನುತ್ತೇವೆ. ಸಾಗರಗಳ ಕೆಳಗೆ ಏನಿದೆ?
kn.example: ಖಂಡಾವರಣ ಪ್ರದೇಶಗಳು ಆಳವಿಲ್ಲದ, ಪ್ಲವಕ ಬೆಳೆಯಲು ಸಾಕಷ್ಟು ಸೂರ್ಯಬೆಳಕು ಪಡೆಯುವುದರಿಂದ ಮೀನುಗಾರಿಕೆ ಸಮೃದ್ಧ.
kn.activity: ಉಪ್ಪುನೀರು ಪರೀಕ್ಷೆ: ಮಕ್ಕಳು ನೀರಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಉಪ್ಪು ಕರಗಿಸಿ ಮೊಟ್ಟೆ ತೇಲಿಸಿ ಲವಣತೆ ತೇಲುವಿಕೆಯನ್ನು ಹೇಗೆ ಬದಲಿಸುತ್ತದೆ ನೋಡುತ್ತಾರೆ.
kn.homework: ಸಾಗರ ತಳದ ಹೆಸರಿಸಿದ ಚಿತ್ರ ಬಿಡಿಸು.

topics.title: Biosphere
topics.summary: The biosphere is the narrow zone where land, water and air meet and life exists.
notes: The biosphere is the narrow zone where land, water and air meet and life exists.
An ecosystem includes living things and their surroundings working together; examples are forests, grasslands, deserts and ponds.
Food chains and webs link producers, consumers and decomposers; energy flows from the Sun through them.
Biodiversity is the variety of life; it is threatened by deforestation, pollution and poaching, and protected by national parks, sanctuaries and biosphere reserves (Nilgiri).
outcomes: Explain the biosphere, ecosystems and food chains
Describe biodiversity and why it must be conserved

lesson.hook: If all the frogs in a paddy field vanished, the rice harvest could fall. How are frogs and rice connected?
lesson.example: Frogs eat insects that damage crops; without frogs, pests increase and harvests fall.
lesson.activity: Food web game: children link cards of rice plant, insect, frog, snake, eagle and decomposers with string.

questions.a: The zone of the Earth where life exists.

questions.q: Give an example of a food chain.
questions.a: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle (or any correct chain).

questions.q: Name a biosphere reserve that includes Karnataka.

lesson.homework: List ten plants and animals near your home and draw a food web linking them.

kn.title: ಜೀವಗೋಳ
notes: ನೆಲ, ನೀರು, ಗಾಳಿ ಸೇರಿ ಜೀವವಿರುವ ಕಿರಿದಾದ ವಲಯ ಜೀವಗೋಳ.
ಜೀವಿಗಳು ಮತ್ತು ಅವುಗಳ ಪರಿಸರ ಒಟ್ಟಾಗಿ ಕಾರ್ಯನಿರ್ವಹಿಸುವುದು ಪರಿಸರ ವ್ಯವಸ್ಥೆ; ಉದಾ: ಕಾಡು, ಹುಲ್ಲುಗಾವಲು, ಮರುಭೂಮಿ, ಕೊಳ.
ಆಹಾರ ಸರಪಳಿ-ಜಾಲಗಳು ಉತ್ಪಾದಕ, ಭಕ್ಷಕ, ವಿಘಟಕಗಳನ್ನು ಜೋಡಿಸುತ್ತವೆ; ಸೂರ್ಯನಿಂದ ಶಕ್ತಿ ಅವುಗಳ ಮೂಲಕ ಹರಿಯುತ್ತದೆ.
ಜೀವವೈವಿಧ್ಯ ಜೀವಿಗಳ ವೈವಿಧ್ಯ; ಅರಣ್ಯನಾಶ, ಮಾಲಿನ್ಯ, ಬೇಟೆಯಿಂದ ಅಪಾಯ, ರಾಷ್ಟ್ರೀಯ ಉದ್ಯಾನ, ವನ್ಯಧಾಮ, ಜೈವಿಕ ಮೀಸಲು (ನೀಲಗಿರಿ) ಗಳಿಂದ ರಕ್ಷಣೆ.
outcomes: ಜೀವಗೋಳ, ಪರಿಸರ ವ್ಯವಸ್ಥೆ, ಆಹಾರ ಸರಪಳಿ ವಿವರಿಸುವುದು
ಜೀವವೈವಿಧ್ಯ ಮತ್ತು ಅದನ್ನು ಏಕೆ ಸಂರಕ್ಷಿಸಬೇಕು ವರ್ಣಿಸುವುದು
kn.hook: ಭತ್ತದ ಗದ್ದೆಯ ಎಲ್ಲ ಕಪ್ಪೆಗಳು ಮಾಯವಾದರೆ ಭತ್ತದ ಇಳುವರಿ ಕುಸಿಯಬಹುದು. ಕಪ್ಪೆ ಮತ್ತು ಭತ್ತಕ್ಕೆ ಏನು ಸಂಬಂಧ?
kn.example: ಕಪ್ಪೆಗಳು ಬೆಳೆಗೆ ಹಾನಿ ಮಾಡುವ ಕೀಟ ತಿನ್ನುತ್ತವೆ; ಕಪ್ಪೆಯಿಲ್ಲದಿದ್ದರೆ ಕೀಟ ಹೆಚ್ಚಿ ಇಳುವರಿ ಕುಸಿಯುತ್ತದೆ.
kn.activity: ಆಹಾರ ಜಾಲ ಆಟ: ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಭತ್ತದ ಗಿಡ, ಕೀಟ, ಕಪ್ಪೆ, ಹಾವು, ಹದ್ದು, ವಿಘಟಕಗಳ ಕಾರ್ಡ್‌ಗಳನ್ನು ದಾರದಿಂದ ಜೋಡಿಸುತ್ತಾರೆ.

questions.a: ಹುಲ್ಲು → ಮಿಡತೆ → ಕಪ್ಪೆ → ಹಾವು → ಹದ್ದು (ಅಥವಾ ಯಾವುದೇ ಸರಿಯಾದ ಸರಪಳಿ).

kn.homework: ಮನೆಯ ಬಳಿಯ ಹತ್ತು ಸಸ್ಯ-ಪ್ರಾಣಿ ಪಟ್ಟಿ ಮಾಡಿ ಅವನ್ನು ಜೋಡಿಸುವ ಆಹಾರ ಜಾಲ ಬಿಡಿಸು.

topics.title: Basic Concepts of Economics
topics.summary: Goods can be free (air, sunlight) or economic (scarce and priced); services are useful activities like teaching and doctoring.
notes: Goods can be free (air, sunlight) or economic (scarce and priced); services are useful activities like teaching and doctoring.
Utility is the power of a good to satisfy a want; value in exchange is shown by price.
Factors of production: land, labour, capital and organisation (entrepreneur), earning rent, wages, interest and profit.
Demand is the quantity people want to buy at a price; supply is the quantity sellers offer; together they set market prices.
outcomes: Explain basic economic ideas: goods, services, utility, wealth and income
Name the factors of production and explain demand and supply

lesson.hook: Air is useful but free; a bottle of water costs money. Why do some useful things have a price and others don't?
lesson.example: When mangoes flood the market in May, supply rises and prices fall; in the off-season, supply falls and prices rise.
lesson.activity: Market game: groups act as buyers and sellers of a scarce good and see how price changes with supply.

questions.q: Give an example of a free good.
Name the four factors of production.
What happens to price when supply increases and demand stays the same?

lesson.homework: Note the price of tomatoes for two weeks and explain any changes.

kn.title: ಅರ್ಥಶಾಸ್ತ್ರದ ಮೂಲ ಪರಿಕಲ್ಪನೆಗಳು
notes: ಸರಕುಗಳು ಉಚಿತ (ಗಾಳಿ, ಸೂರ್ಯಬೆಳಕು) ಅಥವಾ ಆರ್ಥಿಕ (ಕೊರತೆಯಿರುವ, ಬೆಲೆಯುಳ್ಳ); ಸೇವೆಗಳು ಬೋಧನೆ, ಚಿಕಿತ್ಸೆಯಂತಹ ಉಪಯುಕ್ತ ಚಟುವಟಿಕೆ.
ಬಯಕೆ ತೀರಿಸುವ ಸರಕಿನ ಸಾಮರ್ಥ್ಯ ಉಪಯುಕ್ತತೆ; ವಿನಿಮಯ ಮೌಲ್ಯವನ್ನು ಬೆಲೆ ತೋರಿಸುತ್ತದೆ.
ಉತ್ಪಾದನಾಂಗಗಳು: ಭೂಮಿ, ಶ್ರಮ, ಬಂಡವಾಳ, ಸಂಘಟನೆ (ಉದ್ಯಮಿ); ಅವು ಗೇಣಿ, ಕೂಲಿ, ಬಡ್ಡಿ, ಲಾಭ ಗಳಿಸುತ್ತವೆ.
ಒಂದು ಬೆಲೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಜನ ಕೊಳ್ಳಲು ಬಯಸುವ ಪ್ರಮಾಣ ಬೇಡಿಕೆ; ಮಾರಾಟಗಾರರು ಒದಗಿಸುವ ಪ್ರಮಾಣ ಪೂರೈಕೆ; ಎರಡೂ ಸೇರಿ ಮಾರುಕಟ್ಟೆ ಬೆಲೆ ನಿರ್ಧರಿಸುತ್ತವೆ.
outcomes: ಮೂಲ ಆರ್ಥಿಕ ಪರಿಕಲ್ಪನೆಗಳು: ಸರಕು, ಸೇವೆ, ಉಪಯುಕ್ತತೆ, ಸಂಪತ್ತು, ಆದಾಯ ವಿವರಿಸುವುದು
ಉತ್ಪಾದನಾಂಗಗಳನ್ನು ಹೆಸರಿಸಿ ಬೇಡಿಕೆ-ಪೂರೈಕೆ ವಿವರಿಸುವುದು
kn.hook: ಗಾಳಿ ಉಪಯುಕ್ತ ಆದರೆ ಉಚಿತ; ನೀರಿನ ಬಾಟಲಿಗೆ ಹಣ. ಕೆಲವು ಉಪಯುಕ್ತ ವಸ್ತುಗಳಿಗೆ ಬೆಲೆ, ಕೆಲವಕ್ಕೆ ಇಲ್ಲ ಏಕೆ?
kn.example: ಮೇ ತಿಂಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಮಾರುಕಟ್ಟೆಗೆ ಮಾವು ತುಂಬಿದಾಗ ಪೂರೈಕೆ ಏರಿ ಬೆಲೆ ಇಳಿಯುತ್ತದೆ; ಋತು ಮುಗಿದಾಗ ಪೂರೈಕೆ ಕುಸಿದು ಬೆಲೆ ಏರುತ್ತದೆ.
kn.activity: ಮಾರುಕಟ್ಟೆ ಆಟ: ಗುಂಪುಗಳು ಕೊರತೆಯಿರುವ ಸರಕಿನ ಕೊಳ್ಳುವವರು-ಮಾರುವವರಾಗಿ ಪೂರೈಕೆಯೊಂದಿಗೆ ಬೆಲೆ ಹೇಗೆ ಬದಲಾಗುತ್ತದೆ ನೋಡುತ್ತವೆ.

questions.q: ಬೇಡಿಕೆ ಬದಲಾಗದೆ ಪೂರೈಕೆ ಹೆಚ್ಚಿದರೆ ಬೆಲೆಗೆ ಏನಾಗುತ್ತದೆ?

kn.homework: ಎರಡು ವಾರ ಟೊಮೆಟೊ ಬೆಲೆ ಗಮನಿಸಿ ಬದಲಾವಣೆ ವಿವರಿಸು.

topics.title: Emergence of Business Organisations
topics.summary: Sole trader: owned and run by one person; easy to start, owner keeps all profit but bears unlimited liability.
notes: Sole trader: owned and run by one person; easy to start, owner keeps all profit but bears unlimited liability.
Partnership: 2 or more people share capital, work, profit and loss by a partnership deed.
Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) business: run by the eldest member (karta) for the family.
Cooperative society: formed by members for mutual help on 'one member, one vote'; e.g. milk cooperatives (KMF – Nandini).
outcomes: Describe the early forms of business organisation
Compare sole traders, partnerships, Hindu undivided family businesses and cooperatives

lesson.hook: The corner grocery, a firm of three friends, a family jewellery business and a milk cooperative — how are they owned and run differently?
lesson.example: Village dairy cooperatives collect milk from farmers and supply it to the Karnataka Milk Federation, sold as Nandini.
lesson.activity: Business matching: children match descriptions of local businesses to the correct form of organisation.

questions.q: Who runs a Hindu Undivided Family business?
questions.a: The karta, the eldest member of the family.

questions.q: Give an example of a cooperative in Karnataka.
questions.a: A village milk cooperative supplying Nandini (KMF), or any correct example.

lesson.homework: Find one sole trader and one cooperative near your home and write how each works.

kn.title: ವಿವಿಧ ವ್ಯಾಪಾರ ಸಂಘಟನೆಗಳ ಉದಯ
notes: ಏಕಮಾಲೀಕ: ಒಬ್ಬರೇ ಒಡೆಯ ಮತ್ತು ನಿರ್ವಾಹಕ; ಆರಂಭಿಸುವುದು ಸುಲಭ, ಎಲ್ಲ ಲಾಭ ಒಡೆಯನಿಗೆ, ಆದರೆ ಅಪರಿಮಿತ ಹೊಣೆಗಾರಿಕೆ.
ಪಾಲುದಾರಿಕೆ: 2 ಅಥವಾ ಹೆಚ್ಚು ಜನ ಪಾಲುದಾರಿಕೆ ಪತ್ರದಂತೆ ಬಂಡವಾಳ, ಕೆಲಸ, ಲಾಭ-ನಷ್ಟ ಹಂಚಿಕೊಳ್ಳುತ್ತಾರೆ.
ಅವಿಭಕ್ತ ಹಿಂದೂ ಕುಟುಂಬ ವ್ಯಾಪಾರ: ಕುಟುಂಬಕ್ಕಾಗಿ ಹಿರಿಯ ಸದಸ್ಯ (ಕರ್ತ) ನಡೆಸುತ್ತಾನೆ.
ಸಹಕಾರ ಸಂಘ: 'ಒಬ್ಬ ಸದಸ್ಯ, ಒಂದು ಮತ' ತತ್ವದಲ್ಲಿ ಪರಸ್ಪರ ಸಹಾಯಕ್ಕಾಗಿ ಸದಸ್ಯರು ರಚಿಸುವುದು; ಉದಾ: ಹಾಲಿನ ಸಹಕಾರ ಸಂಘಗಳು (ಕೆಎಂಎಫ್ – ನಂದಿನಿ).
outcomes: ವ್ಯಾಪಾರ ಸಂಘಟನೆಯ ಆರಂಭಿಕ ರೂಪಗಳನ್ನು ವರ್ಣಿಸುವುದು
ಏಕಮಾಲೀಕ, ಪಾಲುದಾರಿಕೆ, ಅವಿಭಕ್ತ ಹಿಂದೂ ಕುಟುಂಬ ವ್ಯಾಪಾರ, ಸಹಕಾರ ಸಂಘ ಹೋಲಿಸುವುದು
kn.hook: ಮೂಲೆಯ ದಿನಸಿ ಅಂಗಡಿ, ಮೂವರು ಸ್ನೇಹಿತರ ಸಂಸ್ಥೆ, ಕುಟುಂಬದ ಆಭರಣ ವ್ಯಾಪಾರ, ಹಾಲಿನ ಸಹಕಾರ ಸಂಘ — ಅವುಗಳ ಒಡೆತನ, ನಿರ್ವಹಣೆ ಹೇಗೆ ಬೇರೆ?
kn.example: ಹಳ್ಳಿಯ ಹಾಲಿನ ಸಹಕಾರ ಸಂಘಗಳು ರೈತರಿಂದ ಹಾಲು ಸಂಗ್ರಹಿಸಿ ಕರ್ನಾಟಕ ಹಾಲು ಮಹಾಮಂಡಳಕ್ಕೆ ಪೂರೈಸುತ್ತವೆ, ಅದು ನಂದಿನಿ ಹೆಸರಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಮಾರಾಟವಾಗುತ್ತದೆ.
kn.activity: ವ್ಯಾಪಾರ ಹೊಂದಿಸುವಿಕೆ: ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಸ್ಥಳೀಯ ವ್ಯಾಪಾರಗಳ ವರ್ಣನೆಯನ್ನು ಸರಿಯಾದ ಸಂಘಟನಾ ರೂಪದೊಂದಿಗೆ ಹೊಂದಿಸುತ್ತಾರೆ.

questions.a: ನಂದಿನಿಗೆ (ಕೆಎಂಎಫ್) ಹಾಲು ಪೂರೈಸುವ ಹಳ್ಳಿಯ ಹಾಲಿನ ಸಹಕಾರ ಸಂಘ, ಅಥವಾ ಯಾವುದೇ ಸರಿಯಾದ ಉದಾಹರಣೆ.

kn.homework: ಮನೆಯ ಬಳಿಯ ಒಂದು ಏಕಮಾಲೀಕ ಮತ್ತು ಒಂದು ಸಹಕಾರ ಸಂಘ ಹುಡುಕಿ ಪ್ರತಿಯೊಂದು ಹೇಗೆ ಕೆಲಸ ಮಾಡುತ್ತದೆ ಬರೆ.

topics.title: Large Business Organisations
topics.summary: A joint stock company is owned by shareholders; its capital is divided into shares, and shareholders have limited liability.
notes: A joint stock company is owned by shareholders; its capital is divided into shares, and shareholders have limited liability.
Private limited companies cannot sell shares to the public; public limited companies can, through stock exchanges.
Multinational companies (MNCs) operate in many countries; they bring investment and technology but may compete with local firms.
Public sector enterprises are owned by the government, e.g. HAL, BEL and BHEL; they serve national needs as well as earning profit.
outcomes: Describe joint stock companies and their types
Explain multinational companies and public sector enterprises

lesson.hook: Thousands of people can own a small piece of a big company by buying its shares. How does that work?
lesson.example: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) in Bengaluru is a public sector company that makes aircraft and helicopters.
lesson.activity: Share market simulation: children 'buy' shares in imaginary companies and track news that changes their value.

questions.a: Shareholders lose at most what they invested, not their personal property.

questions.q: Give an example of a public sector enterprise in Karnataka.

questions.a: A company that operates in many countries.

lesson.homework: List five products at home made by large companies and find out if they are Indian or multinational.

kn.title: ದೊಡ್ಡ ವ್ಯಾಪಾರ ಸಂಘಟನೆಗಳು
notes: ಜಂಟಿ ಬಂಡವಾಳ ಕಂಪನಿಯ ಒಡೆಯರು ಷೇರುದಾರರು; ಬಂಡವಾಳವನ್ನು ಷೇರುಗಳಾಗಿ ವಿಭಜಿಸಲಾಗಿದೆ, ಷೇರುದಾರರಿಗೆ ಪರಿಮಿತ ಹೊಣೆಗಾರಿಕೆ.
ಖಾಸಗಿ ನಿಯಮಿತ ಕಂಪನಿಗಳು ಸಾರ್ವಜನಿಕರಿಗೆ ಷೇರು ಮಾರುವಂತಿಲ್ಲ; ಸಾರ್ವಜನಿಕ ನಿಯಮಿತ ಕಂಪನಿಗಳು ಷೇರುಪೇಟೆಯ ಮೂಲಕ ಮಾರಬಹುದು.
ಬಹುರಾಷ್ಟ್ರೀಯ ಕಂಪನಿಗಳು (MNC) ಅನೇಕ ದೇಶಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಕೆಲಸ ಮಾಡುತ್ತವೆ; ಹೂಡಿಕೆ-ತಂತ್ರಜ್ಞಾನ ತರುತ್ತವೆ, ಆದರೆ ಸ್ಥಳೀಯ ಉದ್ಯಮಗಳೊಂದಿಗೆ ಸ್ಪರ್ಧಿಸಬಹುದು.
ಸಾರ್ವಜನಿಕ ಉದ್ಯಮಗಳ ಒಡೆಯ ಸರ್ಕಾರ, ಉದಾ: HAL, BEL, BHEL; ಲಾಭದ ಜೊತೆಗೆ ರಾಷ್ಟ್ರೀಯ ಅಗತ್ಯ ಪೂರೈಸುತ್ತವೆ.
outcomes: ಜಂಟಿ ಬಂಡವಾಳ ಕಂಪನಿ ಮತ್ತು ಅವುಗಳ ಪ್ರಕಾರ ವರ್ಣಿಸುವುದು
ಬಹುರಾಷ್ಟ್ರೀಯ ಕಂಪನಿ ಮತ್ತು ಸಾರ್ವಜನಿಕ ಉದ್ಯಮ ವಿವರಿಸುವುದು
kn.hook: ಸಾವಿರಾರು ಜನ ಷೇರು ಕೊಂಡು ದೊಡ್ಡ ಕಂಪನಿಯ ಸಣ್ಣ ಭಾಗದ ಒಡೆಯರಾಗಬಹುದು. ಅದು ಹೇಗೆ?
kn.example: ಬೆಂಗಳೂರಿನ ಹಿಂದೂಸ್ತಾನ್ ಏರೋನಾಟಿಕ್ಸ್ ಲಿಮಿಟೆಡ್ (HAL) ವಿಮಾನ ಮತ್ತು ಹೆಲಿಕಾಪ್ಟರ್ ತಯಾರಿಸುವ ಸಾರ್ವಜನಿಕ ವಲಯದ ಕಂಪನಿ.
kn.activity: ಷೇರುಪೇಟೆ ಅನುಕರಣೆ: ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಕಾಲ್ಪನಿಕ ಕಂಪನಿಗಳ ಷೇರು 'ಕೊಂಡು' ಅವುಗಳ ಬೆಲೆ ಬದಲಿಸುವ ಸುದ್ದಿ ಗಮನಿಸುತ್ತಾರೆ.

questions.a: ಷೇರುದಾರರು ತಾವು ಹೂಡಿದಷ್ಟನ್ನು ಮಾತ್ರ ಕಳೆದುಕೊಳ್ಳುತ್ತಾರೆ, ವೈಯಕ್ತಿಕ ಆಸ್ತಿಯಲ್ಲ.

kn.homework: ಮನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ದೊಡ್ಡ ಕಂಪನಿಗಳು ತಯಾರಿಸಿದ ಐದು ವಸ್ತು ಪಟ್ಟಿ ಮಾಡಿ ಅವು ಭಾರತೀಯವೋ ಬಹುರಾಷ್ಟ್ರೀಯವೋ ತಿಳಿದುಕೋ.

topics.title: The Heavenly Parasol
topics.summary: At Princess Amritaprabha's swayamvara she chooses Meghavahana; the divine white parasol of Varuna, lord of the seas, casts its shadow over him — a sign he will rule the world.
notes: At Princess Amritaprabha's swayamvara she chooses Meghavahana; the divine white parasol of Varuna, lord of the seas, casts its shadow over him — a sign he will rule the world.
The ministers of Kashmir offer him the throne; as king he forbids the killing of living beings and wishes to spread this law of peace.
Near the sea he stops a barbarian about to sacrifice a man to Chandika to cure his dying son; to save both lives the king offers his own body and even raises his sword against himself.
Flowers fall on him and Varuna appears: it was a test of his compassion. Meghavahana returns the parasol, Varuna parts the sea for his army, and he wins Lanka's King Vibhishana as a friend.
outcomes: Retell the legend of King Meghavahana of Kashmir
Discuss compassion and the idea of a ruler's duty

lesson.hook: What would you give up to save another person's life?
lesson.example: Test and reward: the illusion tests the king's nobility → he passes by offering himself → the reward is Varuna's boon to part the sea.
lesson.activity: Values debate: 'Was the king right to offer his own life?' Groups argue for and against, giving reasons from the story.

questions.q: What did the shadow of Varuna's parasol mean?
questions.a: That Meghavahana was destined to be a sovereign of the whole world.

questions.q: Why was the barbarian going to kill a man?
questions.a: He believed the sacrifice would please the gods and save his sick son.

questions.q: What boon did Meghavahana ask of Varuna?
questions.a: Help to cross the sea; Varuna promised to pull the waters away.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on 'A true king' using two qualities of Meghavahana from the story.

topics.title: The Boy who Sold Wisdom
topics.summary: Orphaned Nagendra opens a tiny shop with a sign 'Wisdom for Sale'; people laugh, but he is patient.
notes: Orphaned Nagendra opens a tiny shop with a sign 'Wisdom for Sale'; people laugh, but he is patient.
Babu, a rich merchant's foolish son, buys a nickel's worth: 'It is not wise to stand and watch two people fighting.'
When Babu later lands in trouble after ignoring it, he and his father go back to Nagendra and pay for more advice — tell the king the truth when he is in a laughing mood — and the king forgives Babu.

The king buys the costliest wisdom, 'Think deeply before you do anything', and engraves it on his cup; pausing to read it before drinking poisoned medicine, he makes the guilty doctor confess, punishes the plotters and makes Nagendra his minister.
outcomes: Enjoy a folk tale about practical wisdom
Understand how a single idea can change events

lesson.hook: Can wisdom be bought and sold? What would you pay for a good piece of advice?
lesson.example: How one line saved a king: the motto made him pause → the pause frightened the guilty doctor → the doctor confessed → the plot was exposed.
lesson.activity: Wisdom shop: each student writes one 'piece of wisdom' on a card; the class 'buys' the three most useful with paper coins and explains why.

questions.q: What did Nagendra write on his placard?
What wisdom did the king buy for a lakh of rupees?
How did the motto save the king's life?
questions.a: He paused to read it before drinking; the nervous doctor thought he knew of the poison and confessed.

lesson.homework: Write your own 'piece of wisdom' and a short story in which it helps someone.

topics.title: Before the Match
topics.summary: Rajam's M.C.C. team is to play the Y.M.U. in two weeks; he worries about Swaminathan, the team's star bowler, who does not practise.
notes: Rajam's M.C.C. team is to play the Y.M.U. in two weeks; he worries about Swaminathan, the team's star bowler, who does not practise.
Swami tries to escape drill class by claiming he was 'delirious' all night; the Drill Master refuses to believe him.
He goes to Doctor Kesavan for a certificate, but admits he does not even know what delirium means — he guesses it is a kind of stomach ache.
The laughing doctor finds him in the pink of health and will not give a false certificate, but kindly promises to ask the Headmaster to let him leave at 4:30.
outcomes: Enjoy R. K. Narayan's humour from 'Swami and Friends'
Notice how excuses and schoolboy logic create comedy

lesson.hook: Have you ever made an excuse to skip something so you could do something you liked more?
lesson.example: Humour from ignorance: Swami uses a big word ('delirium') to sound ill, but his guess that it means 'stomach ache' gives him away.
lesson.activity: Role-play: act the scene between Swami and the doctor, then discuss whether the doctor's solution was fair.

questions.q: Why did Rajam want Swami to practise?
questions.a: Swami was the team's key bowler and the match was only two weeks away.

questions.q: What excuse did Swami give the Drill Master?
questions.a: That he had been delirious all night and the doctor had told him to avoid drill.

questions.q: Why would the doctor not give a certificate?
questions.a: Swami was healthy, and the doctor could be prosecuted for giving a false certificate.

lesson.homework: Write a polite letter to your Headmaster asking for time to practise for a school match.

topics.title: Anandi Gopal — An Autobiography
topics.summary: An autobiography is a life story told by the person herself; a biography is written by someone else.
notes: An autobiography is a life story told by the person herself; a biography is written by someone else.
Anandi (born Yamuna Joshi, 31 March 1865, Kalyan) was married at nine; her husband Gopal Rao, a supporter of women's education, taught her himself as they moved from town to town.
Grief at losing her own baby for want of medical care strengthened her resolve to study medicine, despite society's disapproval.
She went to America and studied at the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania, becoming one of the first Indian women to earn a medical degree (1886); she returned to India but died young in 1887.
outcomes: Learn about Anandi Gopal Joshi, one of India's first women doctors
Distinguish an autobiography from a biography

lesson.hook: What obstacles might a girl in the 1870s have faced if she wanted to become a doctor?
lesson.example: Point of view: 'I was born on 31st March 1865…' — the first person 'I' marks an autobiography.
lesson.activity: Timeline chart: mark birth, marriage, study, journey abroad and degree on a timeline with one sentence each.

questions.q: What was Anandi Gopal's original name?
How did her husband help her?
questions.a: He believed in women's education and taught her himself, moving cities so he could teach her freely.
She was among the first Indian women to study abroad and earn a medical degree, at a time when girls were rarely educated.

lesson.homework: Write a short autobiography of yourself in about 120 words, using 'I'.

topics.title: A Lesson for Nakul
topics.summary: Nakul, a clever boarder, is a constant worrier and grumbler; after a maths test he panics that he forgot to write his name.
notes: Nakul, a clever boarder, is a constant worrier and grumbler; after a maths test he panics that he forgot to write his name.
Akash, a new boy, calmly takes him to the teacher to check, helps him learn his lines for the Annual Day play, and cheers him on.
At a picnic Nakul overhears the masters praising Akash — cheerful and helpful despite a lame leg — and remembers the pain he had seen in Akash's eyes.
Nakul apologises; Akash explains that his grandmother taught him to look for 'a gleam of light' behind grey clouds — Nakul learns to stop being a 'wet blanket'.
outcomes: Understand how a positive outlook helps us face difficulties
Notice character change in a story

lesson.hook: Do you know someone who stays cheerful even when things are hard for them?
lesson.example: Two outlooks: Nakul — 'It's sure to rain' (sees the dark side); Akash — 'The sun will come out soon' (sees the bright side).
lesson.activity: Silver-lining cards: each student writes a small problem on a card; a partner writes one positive way to look at it.

questions.q: What mistake did Nakul think he had made in the exam?
questions.a: He thought he had forgotten to write his name or roll number.

questions.q: How did Akash help Nakul before the Annual Day?
questions.a: He rehearsed Nakul's lines with him until he was word-perfect.

questions.q: What did Nakul learn from Akash?
questions.a: To stay cheerful and positive despite difficulties.

lesson.homework: Write a diary entry as Nakul on the evening he apologised to Akash.

topics.title: The Model Millionaire
topics.summary: Handsome, kind but penniless Hughie Erskine loves Laura Merton; her father will allow the marriage only if Hughie has £10,000.
notes: Handsome, kind but penniless Hughie Erskine loves Laura Merton; her father will allow the marriage only if Hughie has £10,000.
In his painter friend Alan Trevor's studio he sees a ragged old 'beggar' model and, out of pity, gives him his only sovereign.
Trevor later reveals the model was Baron Hausberg, one of the richest men in Europe, who had posed as a beggar for a painting.
Next morning the Baron's messenger brings Hughie a wedding present of £10,000 for 'Hughie and Laura' — a model millionaire indeed.
outcomes: Enjoy Oscar Wilde's story with an ironic twist
Understand irony and kindness rewarded

lesson.hook: Would you give your last coin to a beggar you had never met?
lesson.example: Irony: Hughie pities a 'beggar' who is actually a millionaire — and the poor man ends up being rewarded by the rich 'beggar'.
lesson.activity: Twist-ending hunt: in groups, recall another story with a surprise ending and explain the twist to the class.

questions.q: What condition did the Colonel set for Hughie?
questions.a: Hughie must have £10,000 of his own before he could marry Laura.

questions.q: What did Hughie give the beggar-model?

questions.a: Baron Hausberg, a very rich man, who then sent Hughie £10,000 as a wedding gift.

lesson.homework: Explain in a paragraph why the title 'The Model Millionaire' has two meanings.

topics.title: The Great Sacrifice (Play)
topics.summary: After the Rana's death, the ambitious Banbir rules Mewar for the infant prince Udai Singh; nobles fear him and there is unrest.
notes: After the Rana's death, the ambitious Banbir rules Mewar for the infant prince Udai Singh; nobles fear him and there is unrest.
Panna, the prince's nurse, cares for Udai Singh alongside her own baby son of the same age.
Learning that Banbir is coming to kill the prince, Panna has Udai Singh carried to safety secretly and lays her own son in the prince's bed.
Banbir kills Panna's son believing him to be the prince; Panna silently bears the loss so that the heir of Mewar lives — the 'great sacrifice'.
outcomes: Read a play about Panna Dai's loyalty to Mewar
Discuss sacrifice and duty

lesson.hook: What is the greatest sacrifice a person can make for their duty?
lesson.example: Parallel from the pre-reading: Kunti asks Karna for a boon and he gives it for his mother; Panna gives her own son for her duty to the kingdom.
lesson.activity: Freeze-frame: groups present the play's key moments as still pictures; the class names the emotion in each.

questions.a: The late Rana's son and Udai Singh's half-brother, who was ruling Mewar and wanted the throne.

questions.q: How did Panna save the prince?
questions.a: She sent him away secretly and put her own son in the prince's bed.

questions.q: Why is the play called 'The Great Sacrifice'?
questions.a: Panna sacrificed her own son to save the prince and the future of Mewar.

lesson.homework: Write Panna's thoughts in ten lines on the night of the sacrifice.

topics.title: The Woman on Platform 8
topics.summary: Twelve-year-old Arun waits alone at Ambala station at night to change trains to his boarding school.
notes: Twelve-year-old Arun waits alone at Ambala station at night to change trains to his boarding school.
A simply dressed woman in a white sari with a kind face talks to him, takes him to eat, and stays with him till his train comes — without asking anything.
Arun's schoolmate Satish's mother, fussy and patronising, assumes the woman is Arun's mother and looks down on her plainness.
Arun does not give her away; he kisses her cheek and says 'Good-bye, mother', watching her until she disappears in the crowd.
outcomes: Appreciate Ruskin Bond's gentle story of an unexpected bond
Notice feelings through small actions

lesson.hook: Have you ever received kindness from a stranger?
lesson.example: Contrast of two women: Satish's mother — loud, showy, judging; the woman in white — quiet, simple, understanding.
lesson.activity: Kindness board: share (in writing) one small kindness you received from someone you did not know well.

questions.q: Why was Arun at Ambala station?
questions.a: He was waiting for his midnight train back to boarding school.

questions.q: What did Satish's mother think about the woman?
questions.a: That she was Arun's mother, and from a poor family.

questions.q: Why did Arun call the woman 'mother'?
questions.a: He felt her motherly kindness and did not want to expose her before Satish's patronising mother.

lesson.homework: Write the story's last scene from the woman's point of view.

topics.title: Benjamin Jones Goes Swimming (Poem)
topics.summary: Benjamin Jones tells his wife he will win the Fourth of July swimming race; she laughs because he hasn't swum for years.
notes: Benjamin Jones tells his wife he will win the Fourth of July swimming race; she laughs because he hasn't swum for years.
In the race he is passed on every side; he is so slow that a crab tries to bite his toe.
The fear of the crab's claw makes him swim 'like a swimmer possessed' and he takes the lead.
The crowd roars, and his shocked wife falls into the lake with a splash — a double surprise ending.
outcomes: Enjoy Aileen Fisher's humorous narrative poem
Identify rhyme and comic surprise

lesson.hook: Have you ever won something in a surprising way?
lesson.example: Internal rhyme: 'Benjamin Jones in confident tones' — two rhyming words inside one line give a bouncy rhythm.
lesson.activity: Rhyme hunt: list all the internal rhymes in the poem (e.g. came/acclaim, place/race).

questions.q: Why did Benjamin's wife discourage him?
questions.a: He hadn't swum for years and she thought he would come last.
A crab tried to bite his toe.

questions.q: What happened to his wife at the end?
questions.a: She got such a shock that she fell into the lake.

lesson.homework: Write a funny four-line rhyme about a race.

topics.title: Leisure (Poem)
topics.summary: The poet asks what life is worth if we are too full of care to 'stand and stare'.
notes: The poet asks what life is worth if we are too full of care to 'stand and stare'.
We have no time to stand under branches like cows and sheep, or see squirrels hiding nuts in the grass.
We miss streams sparkling with sunlight 'like skies at night' and the beauty of a smile growing from the eyes.
The poem has 14 lines in rhyming couplets; its message — a busy life without leisure is a poor life.
outcomes: Memorise and recite W. H. Davies's 'Leisure'
Reflect on the value of slowing down

lesson.hook: When did you last stop just to look at something beautiful?
lesson.example: Personification: Beauty is imagined as a dancer whose feet dance and whose smile starts in the eyes.
lesson.activity: Stand and stare: spend two silent minutes looking out of the window; write three things you noticed that you usually miss.

questions.q: What do squirrels hide in the grass?
What does the poet say we miss in broad daylight?
questions.a: Streams full of sparkling light, like stars in the night sky.

questions.q: What kind of life does the poet call 'poor'?
questions.a: A life so full of care that there is no time to stand and stare.

lesson.homework: Learn the poem by heart and write a paragraph on how you spend your leisure time.

topics.title: After Apple-Picking (Poem)
topics.summary: The speaker has finished picking apples; his ladder still points toward heaven, a barrel lies unfilled and a few apples remain on the bough.
notes: The speaker has finished picking apples; his ladder still points toward heaven, a barrel lies unfilled and a few apples remain on the bough.
Drowsy at nightfall, he recalls looking through a thin sheet of ice from the trough, and knows his dreams will be full of apples.
He still feels the ladder's pressure on his foot and hears apples rumbling into the cellar — he is tired of 'the great harvest I myself desired'.
Every fallen apple went to the cider heap as worthless; the poem reflects on exhaustion, over-work and the kind of sleep that follows.
outcomes: Understand Robert Frost's reflective poem on work and weariness
Notice imagery of sleep and harvest

lesson.hook: How do you feel after finishing a long, tiring task you once looked forward to?
lesson.example: Sense images: sight (magnified apples), touch (ache of the ladder-rung), sound (rumbling apples) — the harvest follows him into sleep.
lesson.activity: Work and rest chart: list three tasks you enjoy and three that tire you; discuss how to balance work and rest.

questions.q: What remains unfinished in the orchard?
questions.a: A barrel not filled and two or three apples not picked.

questions.q: What does the speaker keep hearing?
questions.a: Loads of apples rumbling into the cellar bin.

questions.q: Why do fallen apples go to the cider heap?
questions.a: Even if unbruised, fallen apples are treated as worthless.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on a time you felt 'overtired of the great harvest I myself desired'.

topics.title: Palanquin Bearers (Poem)
topics.summary: Sarojini Naidu, the 'Nightingale of India', was also a freedom fighter and the first woman governor of an Indian state.
notes: Sarojini Naidu, the 'Nightingale of India', was also a freedom fighter and the first woman governor of an Indian state.
The bearers carry the bride lightly and gaily, singing as they go.
A chain of similes: she sways like a flower, skims like a bird, floats like a laugh, hangs like a star, springs like a beam, falls like a tear.
The refrain 'We bear her along like a pearl on a string' shows how precious and delicate she is to them.
outcomes: Memorise Sarojini Naidu's lyrical 'Palanquin Bearers'
Identify similes and rhythm

lesson.hook: Imagine carrying a bride in a palanquin. How would you walk, and what would you sing?
lesson.example: Simile: 'She sways like a flower in the wind of our song' — the gentle swaying of the palanquin compared to a flower in the breeze.
lesson.activity: Movement poem: recite the poem in a group while walking in slow rhythm, as if carrying a palanquin.

questions.q: How do the bearers carry the bride?
questions.a: Lightly, gaily and softly, while singing.

questions.q: Why is the bride compared to 'a pearl on a string'?
questions.a: She is precious and delicate, and swings gently like a pearl.

questions.q: Name two similes from the poem.
questions.a: 'Sways like a flower', 'skims like a bird' (also 'hangs like a star', 'falls like a tear').

lesson.homework: Learn the poem by heart and list all the similes in it.

topics.title: Modern Machinery (Poem)
topics.summary: Rudyard Kipling (born in Bombay, Nobel Prize 1907) lets machines speak: they were dug from mines, melted, hammered and filed to fit.
notes: Rudyard Kipling (born in Bombay, Nobel Prize 1907) lets machines speak: they were dug from mines, melted, hammered and filed to fit.
Given only water, coal, oil and a little play, they will serve us 'four and twenty hours a day' — pulling, printing, flying, counting, writing.
But they live by a strict law: they cannot understand a lie, nor love, pity or forgive — a slip in handling them can kill.
Though their smoke may hide the sky, it will pass; for all their power, machines are 'nothing more than children of your brain'.
outcomes: Understand Kipling's poem in the voice of machines
Discuss the proper use and limits of technology

lesson.hook: Can a machine love, forgive or understand a lie?
lesson.example: Message in two halves: machines are powerful servants (stanzas 1–3) but merciless if misused (stanza 4) — and still only human creations (stanza 5).
lesson.activity: Safety poster: design a poster of five safety rules for using a machine at home (mixer, iron, bicycle, etc.).

questions.q: What do the machines ask for?
questions.a: Water, coal, oil and a thousandth of an inch of play.

questions.q: Why does the poet call machines 'children of your brain'?
questions.a: Because humans invented and made them with their minds.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on 'Machines — good servants, bad masters'.

topics.title: Imagination (Poem)
topics.summary: The speaker remembers playing pirate and cowboy as a child — simple games that made him happy.
notes: The speaker remembers playing pirate and cowboy as a child — simple games that made him happy.
Reading let him escape the daily grind: living with Eskimos, flying to the moon with Jules Verne.
He explored Africa with Dr. Livingstone and hid with Huckleberry Finn in America, becoming a hero in his fantasy world.

Growing up made him serious, but he still loves mystery — his message is to keep imagination alive. (The textbook credits it to George Bernard Shaw, the Irish playwright who won both a Nobel Prize and an Oscar.)
outcomes: Memorise a poem about the joys of reading and imagination
Recall famous books mentioned in it

lesson.hook: Which book took your imagination to a far-away place?
lesson.example: Books as vehicles: a Jules Verne novel = rocket to the moon; a travel book = journey with Livingstone; Huckleberry Finn = adventure on the Mississippi.
lesson.activity: Book passport: make a 'passport' page listing three places you have 'visited' through books.

questions.q: What games did the poet play as a child?
Who was his guide in the forests of Africa?

questions.a: Keep your love of imagination and mystery alive even when you grow up.

lesson.homework: Learn the poem by heart and write about a book that took you on an imaginary journey.

topics.title: The Bees (Poem)
topics.summary: The lines (from Shakespeare's 'Henry V') say bees teach 'the art of order' to a kingdom by a rule of nature.
notes: The lines (from Shakespeare's 'Henry V') say bees teach 'the art of order' to a kingdom by a rule of nature.
Some bees are like magistrates who correct at home, others like merchants trading abroad, and others like soldiers armed with stings raiding the summer buds.
The 'emperor' watches masons build golden roofs, citizens knead honey and porters crowd in with heavy loads.
The stern judge hands over the lazy, yawning drone for punishment — every member has a duty.
outcomes: Read Shakespeare's lines comparing a beehive to a kingdom
Understand extended metaphor

lesson.hook: How do bees work together in a hive? Is there a leader?
lesson.example: Extended metaphor: the whole hive = a kingdom; worker bees = soldiers, merchants, masons, porters; the drone = the idler who is punished.
lesson.activity: Class as a hive: assign 'bee roles' (cleaners, messengers, monitors) for a week and discuss how order helped.

questions.a: The art of order to a peopled kingdom.
Bees armed with stings who gather from summer buds.
The lazy, yawning drone is handed over for punishment.

lesson.homework: Make a table of the different 'jobs' of bees in the poem and their human equals.

topics.title: The Cloud (Poem)
topics.summary: Percy Bysshe Shelley lets the cloud speak: it brings showers to thirsty flowers and shade to leaves at noon.
notes: Percy Bysshe Shelley lets the cloud speak: it brings showers to thirsty flowers and shade to leaves at noon.
It shakes dew to waken buds, lashes the plains with hail and melts it into rain, laughing as it passes in thunder.
'I am the daughter of Earth and Water, and the nursling of the Sky' — it passes through ocean and shore and changes but cannot die.
After rain, when the sky is clear, the cloud silently laughs at its own 'cenotaph' — and rises again like a child from the womb.
outcomes: Memorise Shelley's 'The Cloud' and understand personification
Link the poem to the water cycle

lesson.hook: If a cloud could speak, what would it say about itself?
lesson.example: Water cycle in poetry: evaporation ('from the seas and the streams'), condensation (cloud forms), precipitation (rain/hail), and repeat ('I change, but I cannot die').
lesson.activity: Cloud diary: observe the sky for a week and record the cloud type (cumulus, stratus, nimbus) each day.

questions.q: Who is the 'I' in the poem?
How is the cloud related to Earth, Water and Sky?
questions.a: It is the daughter of Earth and Water and the nursling of the Sky.

questions.q: What does 'I change, but I cannot die' mean?
questions.a: The cloud turns into rain and back into cloud endlessly — the water cycle.

lesson.homework: Learn the first two stanzas by heart and draw the water cycle with lines from the poem as labels.

topics.title: King Sindbad and his Falcon (Supplementary)
topics.summary: In this supplementary reading, King Sindbad loves hunting; his pet falcon never leaves his fist and wears a golden cup to drink from.
notes: In this supplementary reading, King Sindbad loves hunting; his pet falcon never leaves his fist and wears a golden cup to drink from.
A gazelle leaps over the king's head and escapes; he chases it, and the falcon blinds it so the king can catch it.
Thirsty in a waterless place, the king fills the cup with liquid dripping from a tree; the falcon upsets it again and again, even when offered to the horse.
In fury the king cuts off the falcon's wings — then sees a poisonous viper in the tree dripping venom; the loyal falcon dies and the king weeps with remorse.
outcomes: Read a tale from the Arabian Nights about haste and regret
Discuss the danger of acting in anger

lesson.hook: Have you ever been angry with someone and later found they were trying to help you?
lesson.example: Cause and effect: anger without thought → injury to a friend → discovery of the truth → lifelong regret.
lesson.activity: Pause-and-think chart: list three situations where acting in anger could hurt someone and a calmer response for each.

questions.q: What did the falcon wear around her neck?
questions.a: A golden cup for drinking during the hunt.

questions.q: Why did the falcon keep upsetting the cup?
questions.a: The liquid was venom dripping from a viper in the tree.

questions.q: How did the king feel at the end?
questions.a: Deeply remorseful for killing his loyal falcon who had saved his life.

lesson.homework: Write a moral for this story and a short incident from life that shows the same moral.

topics.title: The Broken Gate (Supplementary)
topics.summary: In this supplementary reading, old Mr. Twinkle needs a boy to help in his shop after school; five boys come, including small, ragged Jack.
notes: In this supplementary reading, old Mr. Twinkle needs a boy to help in his shop after school; five boys come, including small, ragged Jack.
While waiting, all five swing on the old yard gate until it breaks.
Jack wants to own up, but the others refuse; in the interviews they all deny knowing anything about the gate.
Jack stays back to try to mend it and admits he was swinging on it, without naming the others; Mr. Twinkle had seen everything — and chooses honest Jack for the job.
outcomes: Read Enid Blyton's story about honesty
Discuss owning up to mistakes

lesson.hook: If you broke something and no one saw, would you tell?
lesson.example: Two kinds of loyalty: Jack is honest about himself but loyal to his friends by not naming them — both values together win Mr. Twinkle's trust.
lesson.activity: Honesty scenarios: discuss the pre-reading situations (copying, found money, overcharging) and agree on the honest action for each.

questions.q: Why did old man Twinkle need a boy?
questions.a: To help in his shop and drive Jenny the pony with the goods cart after school.

questions.q: What did the other boys do about the gate?
questions.a: They pretended they knew nothing about it.

questions.q: Why did Mr. Twinkle choose Jack?
questions.a: Jack owned up honestly and even tried to mend the gate.

lesson.homework: Write about a time when telling the truth was hard but right.

topics.title: The Miser (Supplementary)
topics.summary: In this supplementary reading by Shantini Govindan, rich Surender owns three barns of treasure but lets his family eat gruel and wear the cheapest clothes.
notes: In this supplementary reading by Shantini Govindan, rich Surender owns three barns of treasure but lets his family eat gruel and wear the cheapest clothes.
Craving a ladoo, he refuses to let his wife make any for the children, neighbours or even herself — she makes just one, and he eats it alone.
Sakka, king of the gods, takes Surender's form and throws open the barns to the townsfolk, telling them to chase away any 'impostor'.
The real Surender is chased to the king; his wife tests both with a question on generosity — Sakka says 'To all!', the miser says 'To none!' — and the miser's selfishness is exposed.
outcomes: Enjoy a humorous tale about miserliness
Discuss generosity and sharing

lesson.hook: Is it good to save everything and share nothing?
lesson.example: The test question: 'Is it better to be generous to yourself, family, neighbours or servants?' — the answer reveals the true character of each 'Surender'.
lesson.activity: Sharing circle: bring one small thing (a story, a snack, a skill) to share with the class and explain why sharing felt good.

questions.q: How did Surender treat his family?
questions.a: He fed them gruel and bought the cheapest clothes to save money.

questions.q: How did Sakka teach Surender a lesson?
questions.a: He took Surender's form and gave away the treasure to the townsfolk.

questions.q: How did Vandana tell the two apart?
questions.a: By asking each whom one should be generous to — Sakka said 'To all', Surender said 'To none'.

lesson.homework: Write a short speech on 'The joy of sharing'.

chapters.title: A Day in the Ashram · Beauty

topics.title: A Day in the Ashram · Beauty
topics.summary: C. F. Andrews, an English priest, educator and close friend of Gandhiji, describes a day at Shantiniketan, the ashram-school founded by Rabindranath Tagore.
notes: C. F. Andrews, an English priest, educator and close friend of Gandhiji, describes a day at Shantiniketan, the ashram-school founded by Rabindranath Tagore.
Before sunrise the choristers go round singing the morning hymn; each boy then sits alone on his asan to meditate before the school hymn.
Classes of eight to ten boys sit with their teacher in the open air under trees; very few books are used — much learning happens through conversation and questions.
The poem 'Beauty' says beauty is seen in sunlight, trees, birds and growing corn, heard in the wind and rain and in earnest songs — and it lives within ourselves too.
outcomes: Learn about joyful learning at Tagore's Shantiniketan through C. F. Andrews's account
Appreciate E-Yeh-Shure's poem on where beauty lives

lesson.hook: What would school be like if classes were held under trees?
lesson.example: Contrast: an ordinary classroom — four walls, many books, big classes; Shantiniketan — open air, few books, small groups, learning by conversation.
lesson.activity: Outdoor class: hold one lesson under a tree in the school ground and afterwards list what felt different.

questions.q: How are classes held at Shantiniketan?
questions.a: In the open air under trees, in small groups of eight to ten boys with their teacher.

questions.q: According to the poem, where can beauty be found?
questions.a: In nature — sunlight, trees, birds, corn — in sounds like wind and rain, in earnest songs, and within ourselves.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph describing your idea of a joyful school. Learn the poem 'Beauty' by heart.

chapters.title: Sir C. V. Raman · The Little Busy Bee

topics.title: Sir C. V. Raman · The Little Busy Bee
topics.summary: C. V. Raman was born on 7 November 1888 in Trichy; though often ill, he passed matriculation at twelve and topped his B.A. in Physics.
notes: C. V. Raman was born on 7 November 1888 in Trichy; though often ill, he passed matriculation at twelve and topped his B.A. in Physics.
Ill health stopped him from studying abroad; he joined the finance service in Calcutta as Deputy Accountant General, but kept doing research in his spare time.
He later became a physics professor and discovered the 'Raman Effect' on the scattering of light, winning the Nobel Prize (1930); he set up the Raman Research Institute in Bengaluru.
'The Little Busy Bee' praises the bee that improves each shining hour gathering honey — so should we spend our time in useful work and learning.
outcomes: Learn about the life and achievement of Sir C. V. Raman
Enjoy Isaac Watts's poem on using time well

lesson.hook: What would you do if your family wanted you to give up the subject you loved?
lesson.example: Raman's persistence: poor health → finance job → research after office hours → Nobel Prize. Passion kept him going despite setbacks.
lesson.activity: Science Day: February 28 (National Science Day) marks the Raman Effect discovery; make a class chart of five Indian scientists and their work.

questions.q: When and where was C. V. Raman born?

questions.a: Discovering the Raman Effect on the scattering of light, for which he won the Nobel Prize.

questions.q: What lesson does the busy bee teach?
questions.a: To make good use of every hour in useful work.

lesson.homework: Write a short biography (100 words) of an Indian scientist you admire.

chapters.title: Jamaican Fragment · No Men are Foreign

topics.title: Jamaican Fragment · No Men are Foreign
topics.summary: On his morning walk in Jamaica the narrator sees a small white boy ordering a bigger dark boy about, and the dark boy obeying.
notes: On his morning walk in Jamaica the narrator sees a small white boy ordering a bigger dark boy about, and the dark boy obeying.
He is troubled all day, wondering whether his race has accepted inferiority even in childhood — his faith in his people is shaken.
Next morning the roles are reversed: it is a game in which the boys take turns being boss; he 'explains' this to a white man at the gate.

The man smiles: the boys are brothers, his own sons — their mother is fair-skinned. The narrator learns grown-ups misread children's play through their own prejudices. Kirkup's poem says beneath all uniforms and borders people are alike.
outcomes: Understand how prejudice can mislead us, through A. L. Hendricks's story
Appreciate James Kirkup's poem on human oneness

lesson.hook: Have you ever judged a situation too quickly and later found you were wrong?
lesson.example: Irony: the narrator lectures a stranger about prejudice — and discovers his own assumptions were wrong from the start.
lesson.activity: Same-and-different chart: pair up with a classmate and list five things you share and five ways you differ.

questions.q: What did the narrator see on the first morning?
questions.a: A small white boy giving orders and a bigger dark boy obeying.

questions.q: What did he see on the second morning?
questions.a: The dark boy was giving orders and the white boy obeying — it was a game of taking turns.

questions.q: What surprising fact did the man reveal?
questions.a: Both boys were his sons — brothers.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on 'We must not judge people by their colour'. Learn two stanzas of 'No Men are Foreign'.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Asked for More · For a Five Year Old

topics.title: The Boy Who Asked for More · For a Five Year Old
topics.summary: Oliver Twist is born in a poorhouse in 1837; his mother dies at once; Mr. Bumble, the self-important beadle, names him and ill-treats the children.
notes: Oliver Twist is born in a poorhouse in 1837; his mother dies at once; Mr. Bumble, the self-important beadle, names him and ill-treats the children.
The starving boys get one small bowl of thin gruel; a big boy threatens to eat his neighbour unless he gets more, and lots are drawn — Oliver must ask.

Oliver walks up to the master and says, 'Please, sir, I want some more' — the shocked master strikes him and raises an alarm, and the board decides to get rid of him, offering money to anyone who will take him.
In 'For a Five Year Old', a mother teaches her child kindness to a snail, but the poet admits adults are not always kind themselves — we preach one thing and practise another.
outcomes: Read an extract from Dickens's 'Oliver Twist' on the cruelty of the poorhouse
Understand the contradiction in Fleur Adcock's poem

lesson.hook: What would happen if you asked for a second helping in a place where food was scarce?
lesson.example: Dickens's purpose: through Oliver's hunger he attacked real social evils of Victorian England — child labour and cruel institutions.
lesson.activity: Hot seat: one student plays Oliver and answers classmates' questions about life in the poorhouse.

questions.q: Why did Oliver ask for more?
questions.a: The boys were always hungry; lots were drawn and Oliver was chosen to ask.

questions.q: What contradiction does the poet admit in 'For a Five Year Old'?
questions.a: She teaches the child kindness, but adults themselves are often unkind.

lesson.homework: Write Oliver's diary entry for the evening he asked for more.

chapters.title: The Swan and the Princes · Somebody’s Mother

topics.title: The Swan and the Princes · Somebody’s Mother
topics.summary: Devadatta complains to King Suddhodana that Prince Siddhartha has taken the swan he shot.
notes: Devadatta complains to King Suddhodana that Prince Siddhartha has taken the swan he shot.
Siddhartha says the swan is his because he saved its life; a kshatriya cannot give up what he has shot, says the king — but neither can he give up one who seeks protection, replies Siddhartha.
The Chief Minister places the swan on a stool and lets both princes call it; it trembles at Devadatta's call and flies onto Siddhartha's arms.
The swan decides the case — it belongs to Siddhartha. In 'Somebody's Mother', a schoolboy helps an old woman across a snowy street because 'she's somebody's mother'.
outcomes: Read a play from Siddhartha's childhood about the right to a life
Enjoy Mary Dow Brine's poem on kindness to the old

lesson.hook: Who owns a wounded bird — the one who shot it or the one who saved it?
lesson.example: Clever judgement: instead of arguing, the minister lets the bird choose — the one it trusts is the one who cared for it.
lesson.activity: Court role-play: act the play, then hold a short class 'court' on another dispute (e.g. a found pencil).

questions.q: Why did Devadatta say the swan was his?
questions.a: Because he had shot it with his arrow.

questions.q: How did the Chief Minister settle the case?
questions.a: He let the swan choose; it flew to Siddhartha.

questions.q: Why did the boy in the poem help the old woman?
questions.a: Because she was 'somebody's mother' — he hoped others would help his own mother too.

lesson.homework: Write an imaginary dialogue between the swan and Siddhartha after the judgement.

chapters.title: All the World Her Stage · Coromandel Fishers

topics.title: All the World Her Stage · Coromandel Fishers
topics.summary: Sai Paranjpye grew up in Pune walking with her grandfather Sir R. P. Paranjpye, a famous mathematician and educationist, who asked her maths questions and told her stories.
notes: Sai Paranjpye grew up in Pune walking with her grandfather Sir R. P. Paranjpye, a famous mathematician and educationist, who asked her maths questions and told her stories.
When she made up her own fairy tale, 'Appa' was delighted; she published her first book of fairy tales, 'Mulancha Mera', at eight.
Books were revered in the family; she grew into a theatre and television director and film-maker, winning a National Award for a social documentary.
'Coromandel Fishers' calls the fishermen to rise at dawn — the wind is their friend, the sea their mother, the clouds their brothers — and to sail out bravely to the sea.
outcomes: Read the life-sketch of film-maker Sai Paranjpye
Memorise Sarojini Naidu's 'Coromandel Fishers'

lesson.hook: Who first encouraged your creativity — a parent, grandparent or teacher?
lesson.example: Personification in the poem: sea = mother, wind = playmate, clouds = brothers — nature is family to the fishers.
lesson.activity: Story circle: each student invents a two-minute fairy tale, as Sai did, and tells it to a group.

questions.a: Sai's grandfather, the mathematician and educationist Sir R. P. Paranjpye.

questions.q: What did Sai publish at the age of eight?
questions.a: A book of fairy tales called 'Mulancha Mera'.

questions.q: How does Naidu describe the sea in 'Coromandel Fishers'?
questions.a: As a mother who will keep the fishers safe.

lesson.homework: Learn 'Coromandel Fishers' by heart and write a paragraph on someone who inspired your creativity.

topics.title: The Emperor’s New Clothes · Machine
topics.summary: A vain emperor thinks only of new clothes; two cheats pose as 'magic weavers' whose cloth is invisible to anyone foolish or unfit for office.
notes: A vain emperor thinks only of new clothes; two cheats pose as 'magic weavers' whose cloth is invisible to anyone foolish or unfit for office.
They demand the finest silk and gold thread and pretend to weave on empty looms; ministers, afraid of seeming foolish, praise the 'cloth'.
The emperor too pretends to see it and parades through the city in his 'new clothes'; everyone praises them.

A child cries out that the emperor has nothing on — the truth spreads and the emperor is shamed. Kipling's 'Machine' says machines serve us tirelessly but cannot love, pity or forgive — they are only children of our brain.
outcomes: Enjoy a play on vanity and flattery
Understand Kipling's view of machines as servants with limits

lesson.hook: Why do people sometimes pretend to see or like something just to avoid looking foolish?
lesson.example: Why the trick worked: fear of looking foolish made every adult lie; only an innocent child told the truth.
lesson.activity: Class play: perform the Emperor's procession; discuss when 'speaking up' takes courage.

questions.q: What was special about the weavers' cloth, as they claimed?
questions.a: It was invisible to anyone who was foolish or unfit for his post.

questions.q: Why did the ministers praise the cloth?
questions.a: They were afraid of being thought foolish or unfit.
A child in the crowd who said the emperor had nothing on.

lesson.homework: Write the story's moral and give one real-life example of flattery.

chapters.title: Luther Burbank · The Axe in the Wood

topics.title: Luther Burbank · The Axe in the Wood
topics.summary: Luther Burbank, an American plant breeder inspired by Darwin's writings, ran nursery gardens and experimental farms in Santa Rosa, California.
notes: Luther Burbank, an American plant breeder inspired by Darwin's writings, ran nursery gardens and experimental farms in Santa Rosa, California.
He created new varieties — a new daisy, a better potato, stoneless plums, a white blackberry, spineless cactus that grew fast for fodder — by patient selection, crossing and grafting.

He was called a 'magician', but he was really a hard-working scientist whose work still helps agriculture and horticulture worldwide; the pre-reading tells of Haji Kalimullah Khan who grew 300 mango varieties on one tree.
In 'The Axe in the Wood', the poet admires the axeman's rhythm, but sees the death of a centuries-old tree — 'a thousand men' cut down in that legacy of wood.
outcomes: Learn about plant breeder Luther Burbank's work
Understand Clifford Dyment's poem against thoughtless tree-felling

lesson.hook: Can one person really create new kinds of flowers and fruits?
lesson.example: Grafting: joining a shoot of one plant onto the stem of another so it grows as one — how many varieties can grow on one tree.
lesson.activity: Seed experiment: plant seeds of the same crop in two soils or with different watering and record growth for two weeks.

questions.q: Where did Luther Burbank carry out his experiments?
questions.a: In nursery gardens, greenhouses and experimental farms in Santa Rosa, California.
Stoneless plums, a white blackberry, spineless fast-growing cactus, new flowers and a better potato (any two).

questions.q: What does the poet see in the falling tree?
questions.a: A great loss — like death cutting down a thousand men; centuries of growth destroyed.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on 'Why we must plant and protect trees'.

topics.title: The Story of Dharmavyadha (Supplementary)
topics.summary: In this supplementary reading, Kaushika, a proud Vedic scholar who had left his parents, burns a crane to ashes with an angry glare.
notes: In this supplementary reading, Kaushika, a proud Vedic scholar who had left his parents, burns a crane to ashes with an angry glare.
A housewife, busy serving her husband, makes him wait for alms and says calmly, 'I am not a crane to be burnt by your glare' — she sends him to Dharmavyadha in Mithila to learn dharma.
Dharmavyadha, a meat seller, greets him knowing who sent him; he explains dharma: doing one's duty, truthfulness, patience, mercy, not boasting — and above all serving one's parents.
He shows Kaushika his aged parents whom he serves with devotion; Kaushika's pride melts and he returns to care for his own parents.
outcomes: Read a Mahabharata story about the true meaning of dharma
Discuss duty to parents and humility

lesson.hook: Is a learned person always wiser than a humble worker?
lesson.example: Lesson chain: pride (burning the crane) → humbling (the wise housewife) → teaching (Dharmavyadha) → change (Kaushika returns to his parents).
lesson.activity: Duty list: list five duties you have at home and one way to serve your parents or grandparents this week.

questions.a: Kaushika glared at it in anger for disturbing his studies.
A meat seller in Mithila who knew the mysteries of dharma.
That serving one's parents and doing one's duty humbly is true dharma.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph: 'True learning makes a person humble'.

topics.title: The Earthquake (Supplementary)
topics.summary: In this supplementary folk tale, a nervous hare wonders what would happen if the earth broke apart — just then a ripe bel fruit falls with a thud.
notes: In this supplementary folk tale, a nervous hare wonders what would happen if the earth broke apart — just then a ripe bel fruit falls with a thud.
Sure that the earth is breaking, he runs; other hares join, then deer, boars, buffaloes, rhinos, tigers and elephants — a stampede three miles long.
A lion stops them with three mighty roars and asks who saw the earth break; each group points to another until the question reaches the first hare.
The lion goes with the hare to the spot, finds the fallen bel fruit, and returns to tell the animals the truth — saving them from rushing to their destruction.
outcomes: Enjoy a folk tale about panic and rumour
Understand the value of checking facts

lesson.hook: Have you ever believed a rumour and later found it was false?
lesson.example: The chain of rumour: one frightened hare → a hundred thousand hares → every species — no one checked the fact until the lion did.
lesson.activity: Whisper chain: pass a sentence along the class by whispering and compare the final version with the original.

questions.q: What made the hare think the earth was breaking?
questions.a: A ripe bel fruit fell with a thud on the palm shrub.

questions.q: How did the lion stop the stampede?
questions.a: He ran ahead and roared three times until the animals stopped.

questions.q: What is the moral of the story?
questions.a: Do not believe or spread rumours; check the facts before acting.

lesson.homework: Write about a rumour you heard and how you found out the truth.

topics.title: Lal Bahadur Shastri (Supplementary)
topics.summary: In this supplementary pen-sketch, Lal Bahadur Shastri was born on 2 October 1904 at Mughalsarai; as a boy he paid a poor mango seller fairly rather than take advantage of him.
notes: In this supplementary pen-sketch, Lal Bahadur Shastri was born on 2 October 1904 at Mughalsarai; as a boy he paid a poor mango seller fairly rather than take advantage of him.
He studied at Kashi Vidyapith, walking miles each day as he could not afford a bicycle, and earned the title 'Shastri'.
In prison during the freedom struggle, he refused conditional parole; when his daughter died he returned to jail before his parole ended.
As Railway Minister he reduced the gap between luxurious first class and crowded third class; later he became Prime Minister after Nehru.
outcomes: Learn about the simplicity and integrity of Lal Bahadur Shastri
Relate incidents from his life to values

lesson.hook: What makes a leader truly great — power, or character?
lesson.example: Values in action: fairness (mango seller), sacrifice (parole), equality (railway classes) — his life, not his speeches, taught these values.
lesson.activity: Quote poster: make a poster with Shastri's slogan 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' and explain its meaning.

questions.q: When was Lal Bahadur Shastri born?
Why did he pay the mango seller more?
questions.a: Selling a hundred mangoes for one anna was a loss for the poor seller, so Shastri paid fairly.

questions.q: What did he do as Railway Minister?
questions.a: He reduced the difference between the luxurious first class and the uncomfortable third class and improved third-class facilities.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on one quality of Shastri you would like to develop.

topics.title: The First Woman in Space (Supplementary)
topics.summary: This supplementary reading tells the story of Valentina Tereshkova of the Soviet Union, who became the first woman to travel into space.
notes: This supplementary reading tells the story of Valentina Tereshkova of the Soviet Union, who became the first woman to travel into space.
Born in 1937 in a village, she lost her tractor-driver father in World War II, left regular schooling to work in a tyre factory and a textile mill, and trained in parachute jumping at an aero club.
Inspired by Yuri Gagarin's flight, she applied to the space school; her daring in parachute training and hard work helped her outshine other trainees.
On 16 June 1963 she flew aboard Vostok 6 around the Earth and spoke from space to millions of people below.
Her flight proved that women could face the demands of space travel and inspired generations of women scientists and astronauts.
outcomes: Learn about Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space
Discuss courage and breaking barriers

lesson.hook: What qualities would you need to be the first person to do something daring?
lesson.example: Firsts in space: Yuri Gagarin — first human (1961); Valentina Tereshkova — first woman (1963); Rakesh Sharma — first Indian (1984).
lesson.activity: Space timeline: make a timeline of five 'firsts' in space exploration with pictures.

questions.q: Who was the first woman in space?
questions.a: Valentina Tereshkova of the Soviet Union.

questions.q: In which spacecraft and year did she fly?

lesson.homework: Write a short speech on 'Women who reached for the stars'.

courses.title: Kannada (First Language): ಕನ್ನಡ ಪ್ರಥಮ ಭಾಷೆ (ಭಾಗ 1 ಮತ್ತು 2), Class 8

topics.title: ಮಗ್ಗದ ಸಾಹೇಬ
topics.summary: ಬಾಗಲೋಡಿ ದೇವರಾಯರ ಕತೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಅಬ್ದುಲ್ ರಹೀಮ್ ಸಾಹೇಬರ ಪೂರ್ವಜರು ಮಗ್ಗದಿಂದ ಶ್ರೀಮಂತರಾಗಿ ಮಸೀದಿ-ದೇವಸ್ಥಾನ ಎರಡನ್ನೂ ಕಟ್ಟಿಸಿದ್ದರು; ಊರಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಹಬ್ಬಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಪರಸ್ಪರ ಗೌರವದ ಸಂಪ್ರದಾಯವಿತ್ತು.
notes: ಬಾಗಲೋಡಿ ದೇವರಾಯರ ಕತೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಅಬ್ದುಲ್ ರಹೀಮ್ ಸಾಹೇಬರ ಪೂರ್ವಜರು ಮಗ್ಗದಿಂದ ಶ್ರೀಮಂತರಾಗಿ ಮಸೀದಿ-ದೇವಸ್ಥಾನ ಎರಡನ್ನೂ ಕಟ್ಟಿಸಿದ್ದರು; ಊರಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಹಬ್ಬಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಪರಸ್ಪರ ಗೌರವದ ಸಂಪ್ರದಾಯವಿತ್ತು.
ಬ್ರಿಟಿಷರ ಅಗ್ಗದ ಮಿಲ್ ಬಟ್ಟೆಯಿಂದ ಮಗ್ಗದವರು ಬಡವರಾದರು; ಅದಕ್ಕಾಗಿ ರಹೀಮ್ 'ಮಗ್ಗವಲ್ಲ, ಕೊರಳಿಗೆ ಹಗ್ಗ' ಎಂದು ಮಗ್ಗವನ್ನು ದ್ವೇಷಿಸುತ್ತಾನೆ, ಮಕ್ಕಳನ್ನು ಸರ್ಕಾರಿ ನೌಕರರನ್ನಾಗಿಸಲು ಬಯಸುತ್ತಾನೆ.
ಇಬ್ಬರು ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಗುಮಾಸ್ತ, ಪೋಸ್ಟ್‌ಮಾಸ್ತರ್ ಆಗುತ್ತಾರೆ; ಆದರೆ ಬುದ್ಧಿವಂತ ಕಿರಿಯ ಮಗ ಕರೀಮ್ ಶಾಲೆಯಲ್ಲೇ ಮಗ್ಗ ಕಲಿತು ಅದರಲ್ಲಿ ಸುಧಾರಣೆ-ಹೊಸತನ ತರುತ್ತಾನೆ; ತಂದೆ ಅವನನ್ನು ಮನೆಯಿಂದ ದೂರಮಾಡುತ್ತಾನೆ.
ವರ್ಷಗಳ ನಂತರ ಕಾಯಿಲೆಯಲ್ಲಿರುವ ರಹೀಮ್‌ಗೆ ಕರೀಮ್‌ಗೆ ಪದ್ಮಭೂಷಣ ಸಿಕ್ಕ ಸುದ್ದಿ ತಿಳಿಯುತ್ತದೆ; 'ನನ್ನ ಕರೀಮ್ ವಂಶಕ್ಕೆ ಕೀರ್ತಿ ತಂದ' ಎಂದು ಕಣ್ಣೀರಿಡುತ್ತಾನೆ.
outcomes: ಸಣ್ಣಕಥೆಯ ಮೂಲಕ ಗುಡಿಕೈಗಾರಿಕೆ ಮತ್ತು ಸ್ವಉದ್ಯೋಗದ ಮಹತ್ವ ಅರಿಯುವುದು
ಸೌಹಾರ್ದ ಸಂಪ್ರದಾಯಗಳ ಮೌಲ್ಯ ಗುರುತಿಸುವುದು

lesson.hook: ನಿಮ್ಮ ಊರಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಕೈಮಗ್ಗ, ಕುಂಬಾರಿಕೆ, ಬುಟ್ಟಿ ಹೆಣೆಯುವಂತಹ ಕಸುಬುಗಳು ಇನ್ನೂ ಇವೆಯೇ?
lesson.example: ತಂದೆ-ಮಗನ ದೃಷ್ಟಿ: ತಂದೆಗೆ ಮಗ್ಗ = ಬಡತನದ ಕಾರಣ; ಮಗನಿಗೆ ಮಗ್ಗ = ಹೊಸ ತಂತ್ರ, ಸ್ವಾವಲಂಬನೆ, ಕೀರ್ತಿಯ ದಾರಿ.
lesson.activity: ಕಸುಬು ಸಮೀಕ್ಷೆ: ನಿಮ್ಮೂರಿನ ಒಬ್ಬ ಕುಶಲಕರ್ಮಿಯನ್ನು ಸಂದರ್ಶಿಸಿ ಅವರ ಕಸುಬಿನ ಕಷ್ಟ-ಸುಖಗಳ ವರದಿ ತಯಾರಿಸಿ.

questions.a: ಬ್ರಿಟಿಷರ ಅಗ್ಗದ ಮಿಲ್ ಬಟ್ಟೆಯಿಂದ ಮಗ್ಗದವರು ಬಡವರಾದ್ದರಿಂದ.

questions.q: ಕರೀಮ್ ತಂದೆಯ ಆಸೆಗೆ ವಿರುದ್ಧವಾಗಿ ಏನು ಮಾಡಿದ?
questions.a: ಸರ್ಕಾರಿ ನೌಕರಿಯ ಬದಲು ಮಗ್ಗದ ಕೆಲಸ ಕಲಿತು ಅದರಲ್ಲಿ ಹೊಸತನ ತಂದ.
ಕರೀಮ್‌ಗೆ ಪದ್ಮಭೂಷಣ ಸಿಕ್ಕು ವಂಶಕ್ಕೆ ಕೀರ್ತಿ ತಂದದ್ದು ತಿಳಿದು ಸಂತೋಷದಿಂದ.

lesson.homework: 'ಸ್ವಉದ್ಯೋಗವೂ ಗೌರವದ ದಾರಿ' — ಈ ವಿಷಯದ ಮೇಲೆ ಹತ್ತು ವಾಕ್ಯಗಳ ಪ್ರಬಂಧ ಬರೆಯಿರಿ.

topics.title: ಸಾರ್ಥಕ ಬದುಕಿನ ಸಾಧಕ - ಡಿ.ವಿ.ಜಿ.
topics.summary: ಎನ್. ಎಸ್. ಲಕ್ಷ್ಮೀನಾರಾಯಣ ಭಟ್ಟರ ಈ ವ್ಯಕ್ತಿಚಿತ್ರ ಡಿವಿಜಿ (ಮುಳಬಾಗಿಲು) ಅವರನ್ನು ಪರಿಚಯಿಸುತ್ತದೆ; ಎಸ್.ಎಸ್.ಎಲ್.ಸಿ. ದಾಟದಿದ್ದರೂ ಅವರು ಮಹಾ ಮೇಧಾವಿ ಎನಿಸಿದರು.
notes: ಎನ್. ಎಸ್. ಲಕ್ಷ್ಮೀನಾರಾಯಣ ಭಟ್ಟರ ಈ ವ್ಯಕ್ತಿಚಿತ್ರ ಡಿವಿಜಿ (ಮುಳಬಾಗಿಲು) ಅವರನ್ನು ಪರಿಚಯಿಸುತ್ತದೆ; ಎಸ್.ಎಸ್.ಎಲ್.ಸಿ. ದಾಟದಿದ್ದರೂ ಅವರು ಮಹಾ ಮೇಧಾವಿ ಎನಿಸಿದರು.
ಬಡತನದಿಂದ ಓದು ನಿಲ್ಲುವ ಹಂತದಲ್ಲಿ ಬಂಡಿ ಹೊಡೆಯುವ ರಸೂಲ್‌ಖಾನ್ 'ಗುಂಡಣ್ಣ ಓದಲೇಬೇಕು' ಎಂದು ನೆರವಾದ; ಅಜ್ಜಿ ಸಾಕಮ್ಮ ಮತ್ತು ಸೋದರಮಾವ ತಿಮ್ಮಪ್ಪ ಅವರ ಮೇಲೆ ಪ್ರಭಾವ ಬೀರಿದರು.
ದಿವಾನ್ ಮಿರ್ಜಾ ಇಸ್ಮಾಯಿಲ್ ಅವರಂತಹ ಅಧಿಕಾರಿಗಳೂ ಅವರ ಸ್ನೇಹಕ್ಕಾಗಿ ಹಾತೊರೆಯುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು — ಶೀಲ, ವಿವೇಕ, ನಿಸ್ಪೃಹತೆ ಅವರ ಬಲ.
